questions.loText: Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics.
questions.reading: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
questions.topic: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.8, Section 8.4 and Box 8.4
questions.question: The head of cyber-resilience at a large UK bank is briefing the board on two forthcoming supervisory initiatives: a regulator-led, threat-led red-team penetration test, and a joint UK/US public-private exercise modelled on Exercise Resilient Shield. Which of the following statements should the briefing include?

options.text: Like most regulator-led penetration tests, the test will be mandatory for all banks, funded by the supervisor and focused on response and recovery.
The exercise will be scored bank by bank, and a bank that fails it will be placed on a supervisory remediation plan.
The test will most likely probe the bank’s protective and detective capabilities; the exercise rehearses information sharing, incident handling and public communication rather than testing the bank.
The exercise will include live play against the bank’s systems, so that the responses of law enforcement and intelligence agencies can be tested.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The penetration test**

Regulator-led tests “are typically voluntary, funded by the regulated institution and targeted at larger, more systemic institutions”. “The majority of directed penetration tests focus on regulated institutions’ protective and detective cyber-resilience capabilities, while a few also test response and recovery capabilities.”

⇒ Expect the test to probe protection and detection.

**Step 2 – The exercise**

Resilient Shield “was not a test of individual financial firms or financial systems, but was designed to improve understanding across governments and industry of information-sharing, incident response handling and public communications”.

⇒ C describes both initiatives correctly.

**Interpretation**

Testing checks controls; exercising rehearses the response and the coordination between firms, authorities and governments. The board should prepare for the test as a control assessment and for the exercise as a rehearsal of communication and escalation.

**LO:** ORR-8 c: Explain methods for supervising cyber-resilience, testing and incident response approaches, and cybersecurity and resilience metrics. • **Reference:** BCBS (2018), GARP ORR Ch.8, Section 8.4 (Penetration Testing; Joint Public-Private Exercising) and Box 8.4

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.8, Section 8.4 and Box 8.4 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-8 c.4)

a.reason: Three errors: such tests are typically voluntary, bank-funded and aimed at larger banks, and they focus mostly on protection and detection.

b.reason: The exercise was explicitly not a test of individual firms, so there is no bank-by-bank score.

d.reason: The exercise did not “amount to a cyber war game or include live play” and did not test law enforcement or the security and intelligence agencies.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain best practices recommended by the Basel committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks.
questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: Workbook A29.1 • S1, S2, S3, S4 • Aug-2026 • Map #50
questions.question: The board of a mid-size Singapore bank has appointed the bank’s CRO as its chief AML/CFT oﬀicer, with a direct reporting line to the board. An internal auditor is reviewing the bank’s revised AML/CFT manual, which covers governance, customer onboarding, correspondent banking and staff training. Which of the following statements in the manual is correct?

options.text: The training module classifies smurfing, splitting a large cash sum into many small deposits below the reporting threshold, as layering, the stage that mixes amounts and patterns.
In the combined role, the CRO as chief AML/CFT oﬀicer is responsible for reporting suspicious transactions and is the contact point for supervisors and the FIU on AML/CFT issues.
Where a new customer’s first deposit comes from her own account at another bank subject to the same CDD standard, the bank may rely on that bank’s due diligence instead of its own.
Because every correspondent banking relationship carries the same level of ML/FT risk, the manual applies identical enhanced due diligence to every respondent bank.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Is the CRO allowed to hold the role?**

Para 24: “The chief AML/CFT oﬀicer may also perform the function of the chief risk oﬀicer or the chief compliance oﬀicer or equivalent. He/she should have a direct reporting line to senior management or the board.” What is forbidden (para 23) is business line responsibilities, data protection and internal audit.

⇒ The appointment is permitted, and the board reporting line meets the requirement.

**Step 2 – Which duties come with the role**

Para 22: the chief AML/CFT oﬀicer “should be the contact point regarding all AML/CFT issues for internal and external authorities, including supervisory authorities or financial intelligence units (FIUs)”. Para 25: the oﬀicer “should also have the responsibility for reporting suspicious transactions”.

⇒ The map’s trap (“the chief AML oﬀicer, not the CRO, files reports and contacts regulators”) is about the role: a CRO acting only as CRO does not carry these duties; a CRO appointed chief AML/CFT oﬀicer does.

**Step 3 – Customer due diligence and reliance**

Para 43: a transfer from an account in the customer’s name at another bank subject to the same CDD standard “may provide some comfort”, but the bank “should nevertheless conduct its own due diligence” and consider whether the previous bank closed the account over concerns about illicit activity.

**Step 4 – Correspondent banking**

Para 9: the June 2017 revision of Annex 2 guides banks in applying the risk-based approach to correspondent banking, “recognising that not all correspondent banking relationships bear the same level of risk”, with a list of risk indicators.

**Step 5 – Stages of laundering (ORR-11)**

Placement covers techniques that disguise the origin of funds, including smurfing (a series of small transactions instead of a single large one, to stay below the reporting threshold). Layering combines placement and extraction strategies with varying amounts and patterns. Integration or extraction gets the money out for use.

**Interpretation**

B is correct. The auditor should confirm the combined role is documented, that STR filing and FIU contact sit with the CRO in that capacity, that onboarding requires the bank’s own CDD whatever the source of funds, that correspondent relationships are risk-rated individually, and that the training module places smurfing under placement.

**LO:** ORR-10 a: Explain best practices recommended by the Basel committee for the assessment, management, mitigation, and monitoring of money laundering and financing of terrorism (ML/FT) risks. ORR-10 b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. ORR-10 c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. ORR-11 a: Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk. • **Reference:** BCBS (July 2020), GARP ORR Ch.10, paras 9, 22 to 25, 43; GARP ORR Ch.11, AML Risk Management

ORR-10 • Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A29.1 • S1, S2, S3, S4 • Aug-2026 • Map #50 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-10 a.8)

a.reason: Sibling swap: smurfing is a placement technique; the definition of layering is correct but the technique is assigned to the neighbouring stage.

c.reason: Scope/condition error: the same-CDD-standard condition gives comfort only; it does not remove the bank’s obligation to conduct its own due diligence.

d.reason: Absolute claim: the guidelines recognise that not all correspondent banking relationships bear the same level of risk, so due diligence is risk-based, not uniform.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank.
questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.question: The head of client onboarding at a Luxembourg private bank is rewriting the identification and verification chapter of the bank’s CDD manual. Which of the following provisions is consistent with the Basel Committee guidelines?

options.text: Clients who cannot attend an interview in person are exempt from identity verification, provided their accounts are placed under closer ongoing monitoring.
For corporate clients, a signed written declaration of the beneficial owner’s identity is accepted as suﬀicient verification, with no further evidence sought.
Confidential numbered accounts go through exactly the same CDD as all other accounts, and the holder’s verified identity is known to enough staff for effective due diligence.
Identity is verified with whichever documents the client finds easiest to supply, because the most widely available documents give the most reliable evidence.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Numbered accounts (para 44)**

Confidential numbered accounts must not function as anonymous accounts: they “should be subject to exactly the same CDD procedures as all other customers’ accounts, even if the procedures are carried out by selected staff”. The holder’s identity “must be verified by the bank and known to a suﬀicient number of staff”.

⇒ C restates para 44.

**Step 2 – Beneficial owner declarations (para 37)**

A bank may require a written declaration of the identity of the beneficial owner, “although the bank should not rely solely on such declarations”; it takes reasonable measures to verify the beneficial owner (para 36).

**Step 3 – Non-face-to-face customers (para 37)**

“In no case should a bank disregard its customer identification and verification procedures just because the customer is unable to be present for an interview.”

**Step 4 – Which documents (para 37)**

“The best documents for the verification of identity are those most diﬀicult to obtain illicitly or to counterfeit.”

**Interpretation**

Every wrong option offers a shortcut the guidelines close explicitly. Confidentiality (numbered accounts) is allowed; anonymity and shortcuts in verification are not.

**LO:** ORR-10 b: Describe recommended practices for the acceptance, verification, and identification of customers at a bank. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.10 (BCBS, July 2020), paras 35 to 37 and 44

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-10 b.3)

a.reason: Scope error: there is no exemption for non-face-to-face customers. Closer monitoring is a complement to verification, not a substitute.

b.reason: Absolute reliance: a declaration may be requested but never relied on alone.

d.reason: Polarity flip: the best documents are the hardest to obtain illicitly or forge, not the most convenient or widely available.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.question: A banking group headquartered in Country H has branches and subsidiaries in six countries. Its newly appointed group AML/CFT oﬀicer is setting out how information and authority will flow across the group. Which of the following arrangements is consistent with the Basel Committee guidelines?

options.text: Branches and subsidiaries send head oﬀice information on higher-risk customers only in response to a specific head-oﬀice request, to limit cross-border data flows.
Significant customer relationships are monitored on a consolidated basis for on-balance-sheet accounts only; assets under management and fiduciary holdings stay with each local oﬀice.
To respect local autonomy, the group oﬀicer coordinates the strategy but cannot give orders to foreign subsidiaries, relying on their annual self-certification instead of on-site visits.
Head oﬀice can require every branch and subsidiary to search its files against specified lists of persons suspected of aiding ML or FT, and to report any matches.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Group-wide list searches (para 80)**

“A bank’s head oﬀice should be able to require all branches and subsidiaries to search their files against specified lists or requests for individuals or organisations suspected of aiding and abetting ML and FT, and report matches.”

⇒ D restates para 80.

**Step 2 – Direction of information (para 77)**

Subsidiaries and branches “should be required to proactively provide the head oﬀice with information concerning higher-risk customers and activities”, and respond to head-oﬀice requests in a timely manner.

**Step 3 – Scope of consolidation (para 73)**

Significant relationships, balances and activity are monitored on a consolidated basis, “regardless of whether the accounts are held on-balance sheet, off-balance sheet, as assets under management or on a fiduciary basis, and regardless of where they are held”.

**Step 4 – Powers of the group officer (paras 75 and 76)**

The group AML/CFT oﬀicer has “the authorisation to give orders for all branches, subsidiaries and subordinated entities nationally and abroad” and checks group-wide compliance “including through on-site visits on a regular basis”.

**Interpretation**

The group oﬀicer is built to see and act across borders: information flows up without being asked for, orders flow down, and monitoring covers every way a customer can hold assets with the group.

**LO:** ORR-10 c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.10 (BCBS, July 2020), paras 73, 75 to 77 and 80

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-10 c.4)

a.reason: Polarity flip: higher-risk information is sent proactively, not only on request.

b.reason: Scope error: consolidated monitoring includes off-balance-sheet, AUM and fiduciary holdings.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the group oﬀicer is empowered to give orders group-wide and verifies compliance through regular on-site visits.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.question: A financial group based in Country H runs banking, securities and insurance businesses. Its insurance subsidiary in Country L, where the legal minimum CDD requirements are less demanding than Country H’s, plans to cross-sell the group’s private banking products to its policyholders. Which of the following approaches is consistent with the Basel Committee guidelines?

options.text: The group monitors and shares customer identity and account activity across all three businesses, watches for customers who use services in more than one sector, and applies sector-appropriate AML/CFT requirements when cross-selling.
Each business monitors only its own customers, and information walls between banking, securities and insurance prevent customer data from being shared anywhere within the group.
Because Country L’s legal minimum is lower, the insurance subsidiary applies Country L’s minimum CDD requirements, since a host oﬀice must always follow host-country law and practice.
Because the three businesses belong to one group, identical AML/CFT requirements must be applied in every sector, whatever the differences in their activities and customer relationships.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Mixed financial groups (para 82)**

Groups with securities and insurance businesses “should have the ability to monitor and share information on the identity of customers and their transaction and account activities across the entire group, and be alert to customers that use their services in different sectors”.

**Step 2 – Sector differences (para 83)**

Differences between sectors “may require or justify variations in the AML/CFT requirements imposed on each sector”; when cross-selling, “the appropriate AML/CFT requirements for the relevant sectors should be applied”.

⇒ A combines both paragraphs.

**Step 3 – Home versus host (para 64)**

“Where the minimum regulatory or legal requirements of the home and host countries differ, oﬀices in host jurisdictions should apply the higher standard of the two.”

**Interpretation**

Two traps run in opposite directions: one says the group must be identical everywhere, the other that the host minimum is enough. The guidelines ask for a shared view of the customer, sector-appropriate rules, and never less than the higher of home and host.

**LO:** ORR-10 c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.10 (BCBS, July 2020), paras 64, 82 and 83

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-10 c.5)

b.reason: Polarity flip: the group must monitor and share customer information across banking, securities and insurance.

c.reason: Polarity flip: a lower host minimum does not lower the standard; the host oﬀice applies the higher one, here Country H’s.

d.reason: Absolute claim: sector differences may justify variations in the requirements.

questions.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.question: The head of financial institutions at a London correspondent bank provides US dollar clearing and payment accounts to 40 respondent banks in 25 countries. After a regulatory review she is redrafting the bank’s correspondent banking policy. Which of the following provisions is consistent with the Basel Committee guidelines?

options.text: Respondents licensed and supervised in their home country are treated as low risk by default, so the bank relies on that licence instead of its own assessment of each respondent.
Each respondent is risk-rated individually against a set of risk indicators, and the intensity of due diligence and monitoring follows the rating, since relationships differ in risk.
All respondents receive identical due diligence, because correspondent banking is classed as uniformly high risk and differentiated treatment would breach group-wide consistency.
Payments routed through respondents are monitored only above a fixed value threshold, because the respondents’ own CDD already covers their customers’ smaller transactions.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What GARP says about correspondent banking (para 9)**

The June 2017 revisions to Annex 2 “guide the banks in the application of the risk-based approach for correspondent banking relationships, recognising that not all correspondent banking relationships bear the same level of risk and including an updated list of risk indicators that correspondent banks should consider in their risk assessment”.

⇒ Individual risk rating against risk indicators, with measures to match, is the guidelines’ approach.

**Step 2 – Apply the general rules on reliance**

Another institution’s checks give comfort at most; the bank “should nevertheless conduct its own due diligence” (para 43), and it never relies on standards less strict than its own (para 69).

**Step 3 – Apply the general rules on monitoring**

Monitoring covers all accounts and transactions (para 28), and FT can move in very small amounts (para 59).

**Interpretation**

Correspondent banking is risky because the correspondent processes payments for the respondent’s customers without knowing them, usually across borders, so it leans on the respondent’s own controls. The answer is not to treat every respondent the same but to rate each one and scale the due diligence: the risk-based approach.

**LO:** ORR-10 c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.10 (BCBS, July 2020), paras 9, 28, 43, 59 and 69 (Annex 2 on correspondent banking)

ORR-11 • Financial Crime and Fraud • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-10 c.6)

a.reason: Scope error: a licence says nothing about whether the respondent’s AML/CFT standards are as strict as the bank’s, and reliance never replaces the bank’s own assessment.

c.reason: Absolute claim: the guidelines state that not all correspondent relationships bear the same risk; group consistency means consistent policy, not identical treatment of different risks.

d.reason: Threshold error: monitoring covers all transactions, and small FT payments are exactly what a threshold misses.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance.
questions.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
questions.topic: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Japanese trust bank is reviewing the performance-measurement pack of the bank’s structured-lending unit. For the coming year the unit reports (JPY billion):

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Expected revenues | 14.0 |
| Direct operating costs | 2.5 |
| Funding transfer charge from treasury | 8.0 |
| Expected credit loss | 1.2 |
| Economic capital allocated | 12.0 |
| Regulatory capital requirement | 16.0 |
| 10-day 99% trading VaR of the unit’s hedge book | 0.9 |

The risk-free rate on JGBs is 1.0% and the effective tax rate is 30%. Which of the following is closest to the unit’s after-tax RAROC?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Return on economic capital**

$r_{f} \text{EC} = 1.0\% \times12.0 = \text{JPY} 0.12$ bn

**Step 2 – Pre-tax and after-tax risk-adjusted income**

$14.0 - 2.5 - 8.0 - 1.2 + 0.12 = 2.42, 2.42 \times(1 - 0.30) = \text{JPY} 1.694$ bn

**Step 3 – RAROC on economic capital**

RAROC $= \frac{1.694}{12.0} = 14.1\%$

⇒ The unit returns about 14.1% after tax on the economic capital it consumes.

**Interpretation**

The denominator is economic capital. Regulatory capital is the wrong twin (an industry-wide minimum that rarely captures true risk), and the hedge book’s 10-day VaR is a short-horizon market-risk number already reflected in the unit’s one-year economic capital (Box 18.3). Both are red herrings.

**LO:** ORR-18 c: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance. ORR-18 a: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital. • **Refer-**

**Source:** Workbook A2.2 • S1 • Aug-2026 • Map #3 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-18 c.4)

a.reason: Used regulatory capital as the denominator: 1.694/16.0 = 10.6%.

b.reason: Added the 10-day trading VaR to economic capital: 1.694/(12.0 + 0.9) = 13.1%, double counting a risk already inside EC.

c.reason: Dropped the return on economic capital: (14 − 2.5 − 8 − 1.2)(0.7)/12 = 13.4%.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Singapore commercial bank is preparing the capital-budgeting committee’s review of a corporate loan portfolio. The committee wants both the after-tax RAROC and the economic value added (NIACC) of the portfolio. The data are:

- Loan portfolio: SGD 800 million, headline yield 8.5% per year; direct operating cost: SGD 7 million per year
- Funding: SGD 800 million of deposits, transfer-priced at 5.5% per year
- Expected loss: 0.8% of the portfolio per year
- Economic capital: 6% of the portfolio, invested in government securities yielding 4%
- Effective tax rate: 25%; the bank’s after-tax hurdle rate: 12%

Which of the following is closest to the portfolio’s after-tax RAROC and its NIACC?

options.text: RAROC 13.6%; NIACC SGD 0.75 million
RAROC 16.6%; NIACC SGD 2.19 million
RAROC 19.6%; NIACC SGD 3.63 million
RAROC 19.6%; NIACC SGD 5.55 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Revenue, funding charge and expected loss**

Rev $= 8.5\% \times800 = 68.0, \text{Funding} = 5.5\% \times800 = 44.0, \text{EL} = 0.8\% \times800 = 6.4$

⇒ EL is the average annual default cost, priced into the spread; no capital is held for it, but it is still deducted.

**Step 2 – Economic capital and its return**

EC $= 6\% \times800 = 48.0, r_{f} \text{EC} = 4\% \times48 = 1.92$

⇒ The capital buffer sits in government securities and earns SGD 1.92 million, which is added to the numerator.

**Step 3 – After-tax risk-adjusted income**

$(68.0 - 7.0 - 44.0 - 6.4 + 1.92)(1 - 0.25) = 12.52 \times0.75 = \text{SGD} 9.39$ million

**Step 4 – RAROC**

RAROC $= \frac{9.39}{48.0} = 19.6\%$

⇒ Each SGD of economic capital earns about 19.6 cents a year after tax.

**Step 5 – NIACC (EVA)**

NIACC $= 9.39 - 48.0 \times12\% = 9.39 - 5.76 = \text{SGD} 3.63$ million

⇒ After charging shareholders’ required return on the capital tied up, the portfolio creates SGD 3.63 million of value a year.

**Interpretation**

The two measures agree, as Box 18.2 says they must: RAROC of 19.6% is above the 12% hurdle, so the portfolio is EVA positive. The hurdle is the full after-tax cost of equity; the risk-free return on capital is already credited in the numerator.

**LO:** ORR-18 c: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance. ORR-18 b: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting. • **Reference:** Crouhy, Galai and Mark, Essentials 2e, Ch.17, 18.4 and Box 18.2

**Source:** Workbook A2.1 • S1 • Aug-2026 • Map #3 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-18 c.5)

a.reason: Subtracted the return on economic capital as a cost: (68 − 7 − 44 − 6.4 − 1.92)(0.75) = 6.51, RAROC 13.6%, NIACC 6.51 − 5.76 = 0.75.

b.reason: Dropped the return on economic capital: (68 − 7 − 44 − 6.4)(0.75) = 7.95, RAROC 16.6%, NIACC 7.95 − 5.76 = 2.19.

d.reason: Correct RAROC, but charged capital at the hurdle net of the risk-free rate, 48 × (12% − 4%) = 3.84, giving 9.39 − 3.84 = 5.55. This credits the risk-free return twice.

questions.question: The head of performance measurement at a eurozone bank is evaluating a two-year acquisition-finance deal. Totals over the full two-year life are: revenues EUR 104 million, direct costs EUR 36 million, expected losses EUR 12 million and funding transfer charges EUR 30 million, all accruing evenly. Economic capital is held constant over the life and comprises risk capital of EUR 60 million (measured at the bank’s 99.97% target confidence level), goodwill of EUR 8 million from the acquired origination team, and burned-out capital of EUR 4 million. Capital is invested at a risk-free rate of 3% per year and the tax rate is 25%. Using a one-year horizon, which of the following is closest to the deal’s annual after-tax RAROC?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Economic capital**

EC $= \text{risk capital} + \text{goodwill} + \text{burned-out capital} = 60 + 8 + 4 = \text{EUR} 72$ million

⇒ Strategic risk capital is part of economic capital, not an optional extra.

**Step 2 – Annualise the deal quantities**

Rev = 52, Cost = 18, EL = 6, Funding = 15 (EUR million per year).

**Step 3 – Annual after-tax risk-adjusted income**

(52 − 18 − 6 − 15 + 3% × 72)(1 − 0.25) = 15.16 × 0.75 = 11.37

**Step 4 – RAROC**

RAROC $= \frac{11.37}{72} = 15.8\%$

**Interpretation**

The deal earns 15.8% a year after tax on the full economic capital it ties up. The 99.97% confidence level is already embedded in the risk capital figure; it is not a further input.

**LO:** ORR-18 c: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance. ORR-18 d: Explain challenges that arise when using RAROC for performance measurement, including choosing a time horizon, measuring default probability, and choosing a confidence level. • **Reference:** Crouhy, Galai and Mark, Essentials 2e, Ch.17, 18.4 and 18.5 (RAROC Horizon)

**Source:** Workbook A2.4 • S1 • Map #3 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-18 c.6)

b.reason: Used risk capital alone, in both the denominator and the capital return: (13 + 1.8)(0.75)/60 = 18.5%.

c.reason: Forgot taxes: 15.16/72 = 21.1%, a pre-tax figure.

d.reason: Horizon mismatch: two-year totals over one year of capital, (104 − 36 − 12 − 30 + 2.16)(0.75)/72 = 29.3%.

questions.question: The head of the RAROC group at an Australian bank is presenting to business heads how a unit’s after-tax RAROC responds to changes in its inputs. The unit’s current figures (AUD million) are: expected revenues 14.0, direct costs 2.5, funding transfer charge 8.0, expected loss 1.2, economic capital 12.0 invested at a risk-free rate of 1%, tax rate 30%, giving a RAROC of 14.1%. Each change below is considered alone, all else equal. Which of the following statements should the head include?

options.text: Lowering the confidence level for economic capital from 99.97% to 99.5% would lower RAROC, because a smaller capital allocation earns less return on risk capital.
A higher funding charge transferred from treasury would raise RAROC, because transfer-pricing charges enter the numerator alongside the return on risk capital.
A one-million rise in direct costs would lower RAROC by exactly as much as a one-million fall in expected revenues, both effects reduced by the factor $(1 - t)$.
A one-million rise in expected loss would leave RAROC unchanged, because expected loss is priced into the spread and no risk capital is held against it.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Write RAROC as a function of its components**

RAROC $= \frac{(\text{Rev} - \text{Cost} - \text{Funding} - \text{EL})(1 - t)}{\text{EC}} + r_{f} (1 - t) = \frac{2.3 \times0.7}{12} + 0.7\% = 14.1\%$

⇒ Every pre-tax item in the bracket moves RAROC by $(1 - t)/$EC per unit; economic capital moves only the first term.

**Step 2 – Costs against revenues**

Cost $+ 1 : \frac{(14 - 3.5 - 8 - 1.2 + 0.12)(0.7)}{12} = 8.3\%$

Rev $- 1 : \frac{(13 - 2.5 - 8 - 1.2 + 0.12)(0.7)}{12} = 8.3\%$

⇒ Both cut RAROC by 1 × 0.7/12 = 5.8 points: identical, and scaled by $(1 - t)$.

**Step 3 – The other components**

Funding +1 and EL +1 give the same 8.3%. Lowering the confidence level cuts economic capital; for example EC of 9.0 gives (2.3 + 0.09)(0.7)/9 = 18.6%, a higher RAROC.

**Interpretation**

Direction is the whole question: costs, funding charges and EL lower RAROC; less capital raises it for a profitable unit. The book stresses that the choice of confidence level “can materially affect risk-adjusted performance measures and the resulting capital allocation decisions”.

**LO:** ORR-18 c: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance. ORR-18 d: Explain challenges that arise when using RAROC for performance measurement, including choosing a time horizon, measuring default probability, and choosing a confidence level. • **Reference:** Crouhy, Galai and Mark, Essentials 2e, Ch.17, 18.4 and 18.5 (Confidence Level)

ORR-18 • Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A2.9 • S3 • Map #3 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-18 c.8)

a.reason: Polarity flip. A lower confidence level significantly reduces risk capital (18.5, Confidence Level). For a unit with positive risk-adjusted income the smaller denominator outweighs the lost risk-free return, so RAROC rises (14.1% to 18.6% in the illustration).

b.reason: Polarity flip on a transfer. The funding charge from treasury is a cost charged to the business unit; it is subtracted, so a higher charge lowers RAROC (to 8.3%).

d.reason: Scope error. “No risk capital for EL” is a statement about the denominator; EL is still subtracted in the numerator, so a higher EL lowers RAROC (to 8.3%).

questions.question:
The CFO of a Canadian bank is resetting the single firm-wide hurdle rate used in RAROC-based capital budgeting. The data are:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Market value of common equity | CAD 6.0 billion |
| Book value of common equity | CAD 3.0 billion |
| Market value of preferred equity | CAD 1.5 billion |
| Yield on the bank’s preferred shares | 7.0% |
| Beta of the bank’s common equity | 1.2 |
| Risk-free rate | 4.0% |
| Expected return on the market portfolio | 10.0% |
| Effective tax rate | 25% |

Which of the following is closest to the bank’s hurdle rate?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Cost of common equity (CAPM)**

$$r_{CE} = r_{f} + \beta_{CE}(R_{M} - r_{f} ) = 4.0\% + 1.2 \times6.0\% = 11.2\%$$

⇒ Shareholders require 11.2% a year for holding the bank’s common stock.

**Step 2 – Cost of preferred equity**

$r_{P E} =$ yield on preferred shares = 7.0%

**Step 3 – Market-value weights**

$CE + P E = 6.0 + 1.5 = 7.5 : 80\%$ common, 20% preferred

**Step 4 – Hurdle rate**

$$h_{AT} = \frac{6.0 \times11.2\% + 1.5 \times7.0\%}{7.5} = \frac{0.672 + 0.105}{7.5} = 10.36\%$$

⇒ Any activity with after-tax RAROC above 10.36% is deemed to add value under the traditional rule.

**Interpretation**

Book equity and the tax rate are red herrings: Box 18.4 weights by market values, and the cost of equity is already an after-tax return to shareholders. (Weighting by book value would give 9.80%, which is not even among the options.)

**LO:** ORR-18 e: Calculate the hurdle rate and apply this rate in making business decisions using RAROC. • **Reference:** Crouhy, Galai and Mark, Essentials 2e, Ch.17, Box 18.4

**Source:** Workbook A2.5 • S4 • Aug-2026 • Map #3 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-18 e.2)

b.reason: Reported the cost of common equity alone, ignoring the preferred equity in the weighted average: 11.20%.

c.reason: Grossed the hurdle up for tax: 10.36%/(1 − 0.25) = 13.81%. The hurdle is the after-tax cost of equity and is compared with after-tax RAROC.

d.reason: Multiplied beta by the market return instead of the premium: $r_{CE} = 4\% + 1.2 \times$ 10% = 16%, giving (6 × 16% + 1.5 × 7%)/7.5 = 14.20%.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Canadian bank is pricing a new CAD 500 million mid-market loan book. The book will incur direct costs of CAD 4 million per year, will be funded at a transfer price of 4.5%, carries an expected loss of 0.6% per year, and requires economic capital of CAD 40 million invested in Government of Canada bonds yielding 3.5%. The effective tax rate is 28% and the bank’s hurdle rate is 12%. Which of the following is closest to the minimum annual expected revenue at which the book’s after-tax RAROC just equals the hurdle rate?

options.text: CAD 32.90 million
CAD 34.77 million
CAD 36.17 million
CAD 37.57 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Required after-tax income**

$h \times\text{EC} = 12\% \times40 = \text{CAD} 4.80$ million

**Step 2 – Gross up to pre-tax income**

$\frac{4.80}{1 - 0.28} = \text{CAD} 6.667$ million

⇒ Tax takes 28%, so the book must earn CAD 6.667 million before tax to keep CAD 4.8 million after tax.

**Step 3 – Components to add back**

Funding $= 4.5\% \times500 = 22.50, \text{EL} = 0.6\% \times500 = 3.00, r_{f} \text{EC} = 3.5\% \times40 = 1.40$

**Step 4 – Solve for revenue**

Rev $- 4 - 22.5 - 3.0 + 1.4 = 6.667 \Longrightarrow\text{Rev} = \text{CAD} 34.77$ million

⇒ The book must yield at least 34.77/500 = 6.95% to be value-neutral.

**Interpretation**

This is RAROC used for risk-based pricing: the break-even yield at which the activity neither creates nor destroys shareholder value under the traditional rule.

**LO:** ORR-18 e: Calculate the hurdle rate and apply this rate in making business decisions using RAROC. ORR-18 c: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance. • **Reference:** Crouhy, Galai and Mark, Essentials 2e, Ch.17, 18.4 and Hurdle Rate and Capital Budgeting Decision Rule

**Source:** Workbook A2.3 • S1, S5 • Map #3 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-18 e.6)

c.reason: Forgot the return on economic capital: 6.667 + 4 + 22.5 + 3 = 36.17.

d.reason: Treated the return on economic capital as a cost to recover: 6.667 + 4 + 22.5 + 3 + 1.4 = 37.57.

questions.question:
The CFO of a US bank is explaining the firm-wide hurdle rate to the board. She notes that the bank’s trade-finance unit is exactly at break-even: its expected after-tax RAROC equals the bank’s single hurdle rate. Data (USD):

- Unit, per year: expected revenues 42 million; direct costs 9 million; funding transfer charge 24 million; expected loss 3 million
- Unit economic capital: 60 million, invested at the risk-free rate of 4%; effective tax rate 25%
- Bank: market value of common equity 9 billion; market value of preferred equity 3 billion; yield on preferred shares 6%
- Expected return on the market portfolio: 9%

Which of the following is closest to the cost of common equity implied by the break-even, and to the common equity beta consistent with it under the CAPM?

options.text: Cost of common equity 10.5%; beta 1.30
Cost of common equity 12.0%; beta 1.60
Cost of common equity 12.0%; beta 1.33
Cost of common equity 16.7%; beta 2.53

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The unit’s RAROC (the break-even cost of capital)**

RAROC $= \frac{(42 - 9 - 24 - 3 + 4\% \times60)(1 - 0.25)}{60} = \frac{8.4 \times0.75}{60} = \frac{6.3}{60} = 10.5\%$

⇒ At break-even, the hurdle rate $h_{AT}$ is 10.5%: this is the bank’s after-tax weighted cost of equity capital.

**Step 2 – Back out the cost of common equity from the weighted hurdle**

$h_{AT} = \frac{CE r_{CE} + P E r_{P E}}{CE + P E} \Longrightarrow r_{CE} = \frac{10.5\% \times12 - 3 \times6\%}{9} = \frac{1.26 - 0.18}{9} = 12.0\%$

⇒ Preferred equity is cheaper (6%), so common equity must cost more than the 10.5% average.

**Step 3 – Implied CAPM beta**

$$r_{CE} = r_{f} + \beta_{CE}(R_{M} - r_{f} ) \Longrightarrow\beta_{CE} = \frac{12.0\% - 4\%}{9\% - 4\%} = \frac{8.0\%}{5.0\%} = 1.60$$

**Interpretation**

The unit just covers a 10.5% value-weighted cost of equity. Check: (9 × 12% + 3 × 6%)/12 = 10.5%. Any rise in the bank’s beta would lift the hurdle and push the unit into value destruction under the traditional rule.

**LO:** ORR-18 e: Calculate the hurdle rate and apply this rate in making business decisions using RAROC. ORR-18 c: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance. • **Reference:** Crouhy, Galai and Mark, Essentials 2e, Ch.17, 18.4 and Box 18.4

ORR-18 • Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A2.8 • S4, S5 • Map #3 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-18 e.7)

a.reason: Treated the break-even RAROC as the cost of common equity, ignoring the preferred weight: $r_{CE} = 10.5\%$, $\beta= (10.5\% - 4\%)/5\% = 1.30$.

c.reason: Correct cost of equity, but divided by the market return instead of the premium: $\beta= 12\%/9\% = 1.33$.

d.reason: Used the pre-tax RAROC (8.4/60 = 14%) as the hurdle: $r_{CE} = (14\% \times12 -$ 0.18)/9 = 16.7%, $\beta= 2.53$. The hurdle is an after-tax rate.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a UK bank is reviewing a proposed GBP trade-finance business line for the risk committee. Its expected after-tax risk-adjusted net income is GBP 21 million per year and it requires economic capital of GBP 150 million. The bank’s equity beta is 1.3, the expected return on the market portfolio is 9.0%, and the three-month Treasury bill rate is 3.5%. Using the adjusted RAROC, which of the following is the correct value and decision?

options.text: ARAROC of 2.30%; reject, because it is below the risk-free rate
ARAROC of 3.35%; reject, because it is below the risk-free rate
ARAROC of 6.85%; reject, because it is below the bank’s cost of equity of 10.65%
ARAROC of 6.85%; accept, because it is above the risk-free rate

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Traditional RAROC**

RAROC $= \frac{21}{150} = 14.0\%$

**Step 2 – Systematic risk adjustment**

$$\beta_{E}(R_{M} - r_{f} ) = 1.3 \times(9.0\% - 3.5\%) = 1.3 \times5.5\% = 7.15\%$$

⇒ Shareholders need 7.15% above the risk-free rate for the nondiversifiable risk of this activity.

**Step 3 – Adjusted RAROC**

ARAROC = 14.0% − 7.15% = 6.85%

**Step 4 – Decision rule**

$6.85\% > r_{f} = 3.5\%$: accept.

**Interpretation**

After the adjustment the hurdle is the risk-free rate, the same for every business line. Equivalently, RAROC of 14.0% beats the beta-specific cost of equity 3.5% + 7.15% = 10.65%.

**LO:** ORR-18 f: Calculate the adjusted RAROC for a project to determine its viability. • **Reference:** Crouhy, Galai and Mark, Essentials 2e, Ch.17, Box 18.5

**Source:** Workbook A2.6 • S2 • Map #3 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-18 f.3)

a.reason: Multiplied beta by the market return instead of the premium: 14.0% − 1.3 × 9.0% = 2.30%.

b.reason: Subtracted the full CAPM cost of equity (10.65%) rather than only the risk premium: 14.0% − 10.65% = 3.35%, then compared it with $r_{f}$ . That figure is RAROC minus the hurdle and belongs against zero.

c.reason: Correct value, wrong benchmark: once returns are adjusted for systematic risk, ARAROC is compared with $r_{f}$ , not with the cost of equity, which would remove the risk premium twice.

questions.question: A risk consultant at an Australian bank is advising on a new AUD equipment-leasing activity. The activity’s expected after-tax RAROC is 12.4%. The bank’s traditional single hurdle rate is 10.5%, the risk-free rate is 3.0%, and the expected return on the market portfolio is 8.0%. The consultant wants to know how much systematic risk the activity can carry before it fails the adjusted-RAROC test. Which of the following is closest to the maximum equity beta at which the activity would still be accepted?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Acceptance condition**

ARAROC $= \text{RAROC} - \beta_{E}(R_{M} - r_{f} ) > r_{f}$

**Step 2 – Market risk premium**

$$R_{M} - r_{f} = 8.0\% - 3.0\% = 5.0\%$$

**Step 3 – Break-even beta**

$$12.4\% - \beta_{E} \times5.0\% = 3.0\% \Longrightarrow\beta_{E} = \frac{9.4\%}{5.0\%} = 1.88$$

⇒ At a beta of 1.88 the activity earns exactly $r_{f}$ after compensating shareholders for systematic risk; any higher beta fails.

**Interpretation**

The traditional rule accepts the activity (12.4% > 10.5%) whatever its beta; the adjusted rule accepts it only if $\beta_{E} < 1.88$. The 10.5% hurdle is irrelevant once ARAROC is used.

**LO:** ORR-18 f: Calculate the adjusted RAROC for a project to determine its viability. ORR-18 e: Calculate the hurdle rate and apply this rate in making business decisions using RAROC. • **Reference:** Crouhy, Galai and Mark, Essentials 2e, Ch.17, Box 18.5

**Source:** Workbook A2.7 • S2 • Map #3 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-18 f.6)

a.reason: Divided by the market return instead of the premium: 9.4%/8.0% = 1.18.

b.reason: Used $\beta_{E}R_{M}$ and compared ARAROC with zero: 12.4%/8.0% = 1.55.

d.reason: Compared ARAROC with zero instead of $r_{f}$ : 12.4%/5.0% = 2.48.

questions.question: The head of counterparty risk at a Dutch bank is briefing the board on how the 1995 Amendment to Basel I changed the capital treatment of the bank’s OTC derivatives book, which is documented under an ISDA master agreement with each counterparty. Which of the following statements should the head include?

options.text: Before 1995, two offsetting swaps with the same counterparty each attracted an add-on, which discouraged hedging; once master agreements were judged enforceable, bilateral netting could reduce credit equivalent amounts.
A net negative market value with one counterparty may be offset against positive exposures to other counterparties, provided each relationship is covered by its own master agreement.
The net replacement ratio divides current exposure without netting by current exposure with netting, so it is at least one and scales the add-ons up.
When the net replacement ratio is zero, the add-on for potential future exposure falls to zero, because fully offsetting positions cannot create exposure later.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why netting was blocked in 1988**

The original Basel I gave almost no capital credit for netting: each swap took its own add-on, so a hedge with the same counterparty raised capital. The reason was that master agreements had not been suﬀiciently tested in bankruptcy courts.

⇒ By 1995 the BCBS trusted them, and enforceable bilateral netting could reduce credit equivalent amounts. That is statement A.

**Step 2 – What the 1995 formula allows**

CEA $= \sum\text{max} ( \sum V_{i}, 0) + \sum(0.4D_{j} + 0.6D_{j} \text{NRR}), \text{NRR} = \frac{\text{net}}{\text{gross}} \in[0, 1]$

cpty $i j$

⇒ Values are netted only within a counterparty, and only 60% of each add-on is scaled by the NRR.

**Interpretation**

In GARP Example 21.3, netting cuts the CEA from 61 to 40.7 (NRR = 5/10 = 0.5). The 40% of the add-on that never shrinks reflects that positions offsetting today can diverge before they mature.

**LO:** ORR-21 c: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.21, 21.1 (Netting; Example 21.3)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-21 c.1)

b.reason: Scope error. Netting is bilateral: in Example 21.3 the −10 wheat option “may only be netted against positive exposures at the second counterparty, not at the first”. Separate agreements with separate counterparties do not net against each other.

c.reason: Inverted ratio. The NRR is current exposure with netting over current exposure without netting, so it is at most 1 and scales the add-ons down (0.5 in Example 21.3).

d.reason: Absolute claim. The $0.4D_{j}$ term is never reduced: at NRR = 0 the add-on is still 40% of its gross amount.

questions.question:
A regulatory reporting manager at a Japanese bank that uses the Basel II Foundation IRB approach is computing the capital for a senior unsecured loan to a highly rated domestic corporate. The data are:

- EAD: JPY 50 billion
- Bank’s internal one-year PD estimate: 0.01%
- Bank’s internal LGD estimate: 30%
- Maturity treatment: the Foundation IRB default

Which of the following is closest to the required capital?

options.text: JPY 0.30 billion
JPY 0.39 billion
JPY 0.58 billion
JPY 7.22 billion

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Foundation IRB inputs**

PD is floored at 0.0003 for corporates, so PD = 0.03%, not 0.01%. LGD is the supervisory 45% for senior claims; the internal 30% is not used. MA uses $M = 2.5$.

**Step 2 – Correlation**

$w = \frac{1 - \text{e}^{-50\times0.0003}}{1 - \text{e}^{-50}} = 0.01489, \rho= 0.12(0.01489) + 0.24(0.98511) = 0.2382$

⇒ A very safe obligor gets close to the maximum correlation of 0.24.

**Step 3 – WCDR**

$$z = \frac{-3.4316 + \sqrt{0.2382} \times3.0902}{\sqrt{0.7618}} = \frac{-3.4316 + 1.5083}{0.8728} = -2.2037$$

WCDR $= N (-2.2037) = 0.01377$

**Step 4 – Maturity adjustment at** $M = 2.5$

**Step 5 – Capital**

questions.question:
The CRO of a South African bank asks a senior risk analyst for two figures for the board risk committee: the market risk capital charge for the trading book under the 1996 Amendment internal models approach, and the Basel II IRB credit risk capital for a large, homogeneous book of unsecured personal loans in the banking book (a retail exposure class). Data (ZAR million):

- Trading book, one-day 99% VaR: previous day 17.0; average over the last 60 trading days 5.0. The bank scales one-day VaR to 10 days with the square-root-of-time rule.
- Backtesting: 11 exceptions over the last 250 trading days.
- Loan book: EAD 2,000; LGD 40%; PD 1.5%; one-year default rate at the 99.9th percentile 11%; average remaining maturity 3 years.

Which of the following pairs is closest to the market risk capital charge and the credit risk capital?

options.text: Market risk ZAR 20.0 million; credit risk ZAR 76.0 million
Market risk ZAR 53.8 million; credit risk ZAR 76.0 million
Market risk ZAR 63.2 million; credit risk ZAR 76.0 million
Market risk ZAR 63.2 million; credit risk ZAR 88.0 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Multiplier from backtesting**

11 exceptions in 250 days is “10 or more”, so $m = 4$.

**Step 2 – The max decision (one-day figures)**

max$(\text{VaR}_{t-1}, m \times\text{VaR}_{avg}) = \text{max}(17.0, 4 \times5.0) = \text{max}(17.0, 20.0) = 20.0$

⇒ With the correct multiplier the averaged term binds; with $m = 3$ the previous day’s 17.0 would have bound instead.

**Step 3 – Scale to 10 days**

MR $= 20.0 \times\sqrt{10} = 20.0 \times3.1623 = \text{ZAR} 63.2$ million

**Step 4 – Credit capital**

EAD $\times\text{LGD} \times\text{DR}_{99.9} = 2{,}000 \times0.40 \times0.11 = 88.0, \text{EL} = 2{,}000 \times0.40 \times0.015 = 12.0$ Capital $= 88.0 - 12.0 = \text{ZAR} 76.0$ million

⇒ Personal loans are retail: no maturity adjustment.

**Interpretation**

Total capital is about ZAR 139.2 million, an RWA equivalent of $12.5 \times139.25 = \text{ZAR} 1{,}740.6$ million. The 3-year maturity is a red herring, because retail exposures carry no maturity adjustment. The Basel 2.5 version of this vignette, with a stressed VaR term added, is workbook D4.2 under ORR-22 a.

**LO:** ORR-21 f: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach. ORR-21 c: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.21, 21.1 (Capital for Market Risks Associated with Trading Activities) and 21.2 (The IRB Approach; Retail Exposures Under IRB)

ORR-22 • Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis • Vardeez: UNTIERED

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-21 f.8)

b.reason: Market side: used $m = 3$ despite 11 exceptions, so max(17.0, 15.0) = 17.0 and $17.0 \times\sqrt{10} = 53.8$; the credit figure is correct.

d.reason: Credit side: reported the 99.9th percentile loss, 88.0, without subtracting EL; the market figure is correct.

questions.question: A risk consultant is drafting a one-page history of market risk capital, from the 1996 Amendment to the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB), for the board risk committee of a Dutch bank. Which of the following statements is correct for the consultant to include?

options.text: Basel II replaced the 1996 internal-models VaR with a stressed VaR calibrated to the most stressful year of the previous seven, alongside its three pillars.
Basel 2.5 kept the 1996 VaR term and added a stressed VaR term with its own maximum and multiplier, so with equal multipliers the charge at least doubled.
FRTB keeps both the 10-day 99% VaR and the stressed VaR, scaled from one-day changes with the square-root-of-10 rule, and adds liquidity horizons.
Basel III added the incremental risk charge, a one-year 99.9% VaR that replaced the stressed VaR for all positions held in the trading book.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What Basel II did to market risk**

Nothing: its innovations were IRB credit risk weights, operational risk capital, the three pillars and the QISs; market risk capital stayed on the 1996 basis.

⇒ A is the wrong-accord trap.

**Step 2 – What Basel 2.5 did**

It kept max$(\text{VaR}_{t-1}, m_{c}\text{VaR}_{avg})$ and added max$(\text{SVaR}_{t-1}, m_{s}\text{SVaR}_{avg})$, each with its own max and multiplier; with equal multipliers the charge is at least twice the 1996 charge.

⇒ B is correct.

**Step 3 – What FRTB did**

It replaced VaR plus stressed VaR with a single stressed expected shortfall at 97.5%, computed from overlapping 10-day changes with liquidity horizons of 10 to 120 days; the $\sqrt{10}$ scaling of one-day changes is the Basel I and Basel 2.5 practice it abandons.

**Interpretation**

Shape A4·S5 in one question: each accord changed one thing about the market risk measure. 1996: VaR enters capital. Basel II: no change. Basel 2.5: stressed VaR added (plus IRC and CR). FRTB: VaR and SVaR replaced by stressed ES.

**LO:** ORR-22 a: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge. MR-18 a: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.21, 21.1 and 21.2; Ch.22, 22.2; Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.18, 18.1 and 18.3

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21 and Ch.22, with MR-18 (Hull, RMFI Ch.18) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-22 a.3)

a.reason: Wrong accord: stressed VaR is Basel 2.5 (end 2011); Basel II left the 1996 market risk rules in place.

c.reason: FRTB does not keep VaR or SVaR, and it uses overlapping 10-day changes rather than $\sqrt{10}$ scaling.

d.reason: Wrong accord and wrong scope: the IRC is Basel 2.5, applies to credit-sensitive trading-book positions, and is added to, not substituted for, the stressed VaR.

questions.question:
A market risk analyst at a Canadian bank is calculating the bank’s Basel 2.5 market risk capital charge for the trading book. The bank computes one-day 99% figures by historical simulation and scales them to 10 days with the square-root-of-time rule. A large position was added to the book two days ago. Data (CAD million, one-day 99%):

- VaR on the previous day: 6.5; average VaR over the last 60 trading days: 1.6
- Stressed VaR on the previous day: 7.4; average stressed VaR over the last 60 trading days: 6.9
- Backtesting exceptions over the last 250 trading days: 4

The supervisor applies, to both terms, the multiplier that this backtesting result permits under the 1996 Amendment. Which of the following is closest to the market risk capital charge?

options.text: CAD 20.6 million
CAD 27.2 million
CAD 80.6 million
CAD 86.0 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Multiplier**

Four exceptions is in the green zone (four or fewer), so $m_{c} = m_{s} = 3$.

⇒ The backtest is clean; a multiplier of 4 is required only at 10 or more exceptions.

**Step 2 – VaR term (one-day)**

max$(\text{VaR}_{t-1}, m_{c}\text{VaR}_{avg}) = \text{max}(6.5, 3 \times1.6) = \text{max}(6.5, 4.8) = 6.5$

⇒ After the position build-up, yesterday’s VaR exceeds three times the 60-day average, so the previous-day term binds.

**Step 3 – Stressed VaR term (one-day)**

max$(\text{SVaR}_{t-1}, m_{s}\text{SVaR}_{avg}) = \text{max}(7.4, 3 \times6.9) = \text{max}(7.4, 20.7) = 20.7$

⇒ Stressed VaR is stable, so the multiplied average binds as usual.

**Step 4 – Scale to 10 days and add**

MR$_{2.5} = (6.5 + 20.7) \times\sqrt{10} = 27.2 \times3.1623 = 86.01$

**Interpretation**

The charge is CAD 86.0 million, an RWA equivalent of $12.5 \times86.01 = \text{CAD} 1{,}075$ million. The 1996 charge would have been only $6.5 \times\sqrt{10} = 20.55$; the SVaR term makes the Basel 2.5 charge about 4.2 times larger, well above the “at least twice” minimum.

**LO:** ORR-22 a: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge. ORR-21 c: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.22, 22.2 (Stressed VaR); Ch.21, 21.1 (Capital for Market Risks Associated with Trading Activities)

**Source:** Workbook D4.1 • S1, S2 • Map #73 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-22 a.8)

a.reason: Omitted the stressed VaR term (the 1996 charge, an intermediate result): 6.5 × $\sqrt{10} = 20.55$.

b.reason: Forgot the $\sqrt{10}$ scaling to a 10-day horizon: 6.5 + 20.7 = 27.2.

c.reason: Skipped the max decision on the VaR term and always used $m \times\text{VaR}_{avg}$: (4.8 + $20.7) \times\sqrt{10} = 80.64$.

questions.question:
The CRO of a Singapore bank asks a senior risk analyst for two numbers for the risk committee pack: the Basel 2.5 market risk capital charge for the trading book and the Basel II IRB credit risk capital for a large, homogeneous corporate loan portfolio in the banking book. Data (SGD million):

- Trading book, 10-day 99%: VaR on the previous day 12; 60-day average VaR 10; stressed VaR on the previous day 26; 60-day average stressed VaR 24; multipliers $m_{c} = m_{s} = 3$
- Loan portfolio: EAD 400; LGD 45%; PD 2%; one-year default rate at the 99.9th percentile 12% Which of the following pairs is closest to the market risk capital charge and the credit risk capital?

options.text: Market risk SGD 38.0 million; credit risk SGD 18.0 million
Market risk SGD 30.0 million; credit risk SGD 18.0 million
Market risk SGD 102.0 million; credit risk SGD 21.6 million
Market risk SGD 102.0 million; credit risk SGD 18.0 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Market risk: VaR term (already 10-day)**

max$(\text{VaR}_{t-1}, m_{c}\text{VaR}_{avg}) = \text{max}(12, 3 \times10) = 30$

**Step 2 – Market risk: stressed VaR term**

max$(\text{SVaR}_{t-1}, m_{s}\text{SVaR}_{avg}) = \text{max}(26, 3 \times24) = 72$

**Step 3 – Market risk capital charge**

MR$_{2.5} = 30 + 72 = 102.0$

⇒ The figures are already 10-day, so no $\sqrt{10}$ is applied. The stressed term supplies about 70% of the charge.

**Step 4 – Credit: loss at the 99.9th percentile default rate**

EAD $\times\text{LGD} \times\text{DR}_{99.9} = 400 \times0.45 \times0.12 = 21.6$

⇒ SGD 21.6 million is the one-year 99.9% loss, which is Hull’s credit VaR; it is not yet IRB capital.

**Step 5 – Credit: subtract expected loss**

EL $= 400 \times0.45 \times0.02 = 3.6, \text{Capital} = 21.6 - 3.6 = 18.0$

⇒ IRB capital covers unexpected loss only, because loan loss reserves are taken to cover EL.

**Interpretation**

Market risk SGD 102.0 million and credit risk SGD 18.0 million: SGD 120.0 million in total, an RWA equivalent of SGD 1,500 million. Each wrong option contains exactly one error, so the pair can be checked line by line.

**LO:** ORR-22 a: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge. ORR-21 f: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.22, 22.2; Ch.21, 21.2 (The IRB Approach); Hull, Credit VaR (CR-10)

ORR-22 • Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis • Vardeez: UNTIERED

**Source:** Workbook D4.2 • S1, S2, S3 • Map #73 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-22 a.9)

a.reason: Market side: used the previous-day values without the multiplied averages, 12 + 26 = 38; the credit figure is correct.

b.reason: Market side: omitted the stressed VaR term, leaving the 1996-style charge max(12, 30) = 30 (intermediate result); the credit figure is correct.

c.reason: Credit side: did not subtract EL, reporting the 99.9th percentile loss (credit VaR) of 21.6 as capital; the market figure is correct.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Canadian regional bank is computing the bank’s Basel III net stable funding ratio for the ALCO pack. Balance sheet (CAD million) and the applicable factors are:

| Funding | Amount | ASF | Asset | Amount | RSF |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stable retail deposits | 620 | 95% | Vault cash | 90 | 0% |
| 3-month wholesale CDs | 240 | 0% | Own-sovereign debt | 150 | 5% |
| 10-year senior bonds | 180 | 100% | BBB corporate bonds | 160 | 50% |
| Common equity | 110 | 100% | Business loans (> 1 yr) | 750 | 85% |

Which of the following is closest to the bank’s NSFR?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Available stable funding**

ASF $= 620(0.95) + 240(0) + 180(1.00) + 110(1.00) = 589 + 0 + 180 + 110 = \text{CAD} 879$ million

⇒ Of CAD 1,150 million of funding, CAD 879 million is expected to remain through a stressful year.

**Step 2 – Required stable funding**

RSF $= 90(0) + 150(0.05) + 160(0.50) + 750(0.85) = 0 + 7.5 + 80 + 637.5 = \text{CAD} 725$ million

⇒ The less liquid assets need CAD 725 million of stable funding behind them.

**Step 3 – NSFR**

NSFR $= \frac{879}{725} = 1.212 = 121\%$

**Interpretation**

The bank complies with a cushion of CAD 154 million of ASF. The 3-month CDs contribute nothing, so replacing CDs with term bonds would raise the ratio.

**LO:** ORR-22 f: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.22, Liquidity Requirements and Example of LCR and NSFR

**Source:** Workbook A32.1 • S1 • Aug-2026 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-22 f.5)

a.reason: Inverted the ratio: 725/879 = 82%.

b.reason: Omitted common equity from ASF: (879 − 110)/725 = 106%.

d.reason: Gave the 3-month wholesale CDs a 100% ASF factor, treating them as stable funding: (879 + 240)/725 = 154%.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a US bank is checking the NSFR figure in a regulatory filing. The bank’s balance sheet (USD million), with both NSFR and LCR parameters, is:

| Item | Amount | ASF / RSF factor | LCR parameter |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stable retail deposits | 800 | ASF 95% | 5% run-off |
| 3-month wholesale CDs (1/3 mature | 300 | ASF 0% | 100% run-off on |
| each month) |  |  | the maturing third |
| 10-year senior bonds | 250 | ASF 100% | 0% run-off |
| Common equity | 150 | ASF 100% | 0% run-off |
| Vault cash | 150 | RSF 0% | HQLA factor 100% |
| Own-sovereign debt | 200 | RSF 5% | HQLA factor 100% |
| BBB corporate bonds | 250 | RSF 50% | HQLA factor 50% |
| Business loans (> 1 yr) | 900 | RSF 85% | HQLA factor 0% |

Which of the following is closest to the bank’s NSFR?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – ASF**

ASF $= 800(0.95)+300(0)+250(1.00)+150(1.00) = 760+0+250+150 = \text{USD} 1{,}160$ million

**Step 2 – RSF**

RSF $= 150(0) + 200(0.05) + 250(0.50) + 900(0.85) = 0 + 10 + 125 + 765 = \text{USD} 900$ million

**Step 3 – NSFR**

NSFR $= \frac{1{,}160}{900} = 1.289 = 129\%$

⇒ The bank has 29% more stable funding than its one-year requirement.

**Interpretation**

The LCR column answers a different, 30-day question about what can be sold; the NSFR asks what funding remains after a stressful year, and its categories differ from the LCR’s.

c.reason: Gave the 3-month CDs a 100% ASF factor: (1,160 + 300)/900 = 162%.

d.reason: Computed the LCR instead: HQLA = 150 + 200 + 125 = 475; outflows = 0.05(800) + 300/3 = 140; LCR = 475/140 = 339%.

questions.question:
The head of balance sheet management at a Singapore bank finds that its NSFR is below the minimum. Balance sheet (SGD million) and factors are:

| Funding | Amount | ASF | Asset | Amount | RSF |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stable retail deposits | 400 | 95% | Vault cash | 50 | 0% |
| 3-month wholesale CDs | 350 | 0% | Own-sovereign debt | 100 | 5% |
| 10-year senior bonds | 150 | 100% | BBB corporate bonds | 150 | 50% |
| Common equity | 100 | 100% | Business loans (> 1 yr) | 700 | 85% |

For its LCR, the bank applies a 5% run-off rate to stable retail deposits. The bank plans to raise additional stable retail deposits and invest all the proceeds in own-sovereign debt. Which of the following is closest to the minimum amount of new deposits needed to bring the NSFR to exactly 100%?

options.text: SGD 45.0 million
SGD 50.0 million
SGD 52.9 million
SGD 161.1 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Current ASF and RSF**

ASF = 400(0.95) + 350(0) + 150(1.00) + 100(1.00) = 380 + 0 + 150 + 100 = 630

RSF = 50(0) + 100(0.05) + 150(0.50) + 700(0.85) = 0 + 5 + 75 + 595 = 675

**Step 2 – Current NSFR and gap**

NSFR $= 630/675 = 93.3\%, \text{gap} = 675 - 630 = \text{SGD} 45$ million

**Step 3 – Solve for new deposits** $x$

Each SGD 1 of new deposits adds 0.95 of ASF and, once invested in sovereign debt, 0.05 of RSF:

$630 + 0.95x = 675 + 0.05x \Rightarrow0.90x = 45 \Rightarrow x = \text{SGD} 50.0$ million

**Step 4 – Check**

$$\frac{630 + 47.5}{675 + 2.5} = \frac{677.5}{677.5} = 100\%$$

**Interpretation**

Every remedy has two legs: where the funding comes from (ASF factor) and where it is deployed (RSF factor). The LCR run-off rate is a red herring: it belongs to the 30-day test.

**LO:** ORR-22 f: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.22, Liquidity Requirements and Example of LCR and NSFR

ORR-23 • High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A32.2 • S2 • self-generated (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-22 f.8)

a.reason: Reported the raw ASF gap, ignoring that deposits earn only 95% credit and that the new asset adds RSF: 675 − 630 = 45.0.

c.reason: Added the 5% LCR run-off on the new deposits as a further stable funding requirement: $0.95x - 0.05x - 0.05x = 45$, $x = 45/0.85 = 52.9$.

d.reason: Omitted common equity from current ASF: gap = 675 − 530 = 145, $x =$ 145/0.90 = 161.1.

questions.question: A model validation manager at a eurozone bank is reviewing how the December 2017 input floors apply to the bank’s IRB portfolios. The bank uses the foundation IRB approach for its exposures to large corporates and the advanced IRB approach for its retail portfolios, including qualifying revolving retail exposures (QRRE). Which of the following statements should the manager include in the review?

options.text: The LGD floors apply under both the foundation and the advanced IRB approach, and a partially secured exposure takes the secured LGD floor on its whole amount.
QRRE revolvers face the same 5 bp PD floor as QRRE transactors, and unsecured QRRE exposures face a 30% LGD floor.
The 5 bp PD floor applies to the large corporates under the foundation IRB approach, whereas LGD and EAD floors bind only on the advanced IRB portfolios.
The EAD floor equals the on-balance-sheet exposure plus 100% of the off-balance-sheet exposure, so no credit conversion factor below one may be applied.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Which approach each floor constrains**

Table 23.3, footnote 4: PD floors apply under **both** F-IRB and A-IRB; “the LGD and EAD floors are only applicable in A-IRB approaches”.

⇒ The large corporates on F-IRB face the 5 bp corporate PD floor; their LGD and EAD are supervisory values.

**Step 2 – Check the retail values**

QRRE transactors 5 bp, QRRE revolvers **10 bp**; unsecured LGD floor **50%** for QRRE (30% is other retail). EAD floor: on-balance-sheet exposure plus **50%** of the off-balance-sheet exposure using the SA credit conversion factor.

**Interpretation**

Input floors act on parameters inside the model; they constrain a bank’s own estimates where it still makes them. That is why the LGD and EAD floors have nothing to bite on under F-IRB.

**LO:** ORR-23 b: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework • **Reference:** BCBS, High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (December 2017), GARP ORR Ch.23, Specification of Input Floors, Table 23.3 and footnote 4

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.23 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-23 b.3)

a.reason: Sibling swap: LGD floors are A-IRB only. A partially secured exposure takes a weighted average of the unsecured floor (on the unsecured part) and the secured floor (on the secured part).

b.reason: Two wrong values: QRRE revolvers have a 10 bp PD floor, and the QRRE unsecured LGD floor is 50%; 30% belongs to other retail.

d.reason: The EAD floor adds 50% of the off-balance-sheet exposure (using the SA CCF), not 100%.
