Which of the following conclusions is correct?

options.text: The AMA may be retained for operational risk, since the bank holds more than ten years of high-quality internal loss data.
The internal CVA model may be retained, provided the bank’s non-centrally cleared derivatives notional is EUR 100 billion or less.
Internal ratings remain available for some exposures, such as retail and specialised lending, but no longer for equities; all remaining models face the output floor.
The A-IRB approach may be retained for exposures to banks and large corporates, provided the new PD, LGD and EAD input floors are applied.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Credit risk**

A-IRB is removed for banks, other financial institutions and large and mid-sized corporates (FIRB or SA instead), and every IRB approach is removed for equities. Retail and specialised lending keep their internal estimates, subject to input floors.

**Step 2 – CVA and operational risk**

The internal model for CVA is removed (SA-CVA or BA-CVA). The AMA is replaced by one standardised approach for all banks.

**Step 3 – What constrains the survivors**

The output floor applies to total RWA, so any model still in use (IRB, market risk internal models) can lower total RWA to no less than 72.5% of the standardised-only figure (ORR-23 c).

⇒ C is the only conclusion consistent with all three steps.

**Interpretation**

This is the C5 S2 shape: the standardised versus internal-models split. In Basel II models spread to credit and operational risk; December 2017 pulls them back, area by area, and floors what remains.

**LO:** ORR-23 b: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework • **Reference:** BCBS, High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (December 2017), GARP ORR Ch.23, Table 23.2, CVA and Operational Risk Frameworks, Output Floor; Carey, Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis, GARP ORR Ch.21 (Basel II)

ORR-23 • High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.23 and Ch.21 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-23 b.9)

a.reason: Polarity flip: no amount of loss data keeps the AMA; it is replaced for all banks. (Ten years is the window for the loss component of the new approach.)

b.reason: Scope error: the EUR 100 billion threshold allows a simple multiplier of the CCR charge, not an internal model.

d.reason: Input floors constrain models that remain; they do not restore the A-IRB for banks and large corporates.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.question: A regulatory policy analyst at a Nordic bank is explaining to the board how the output floor in the December 2017 Basel III reforms differs from the floor it replaces. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The Basel II floor was set at 72.5% of Basel I capital requirements; the new floor raises the calibration to 80% of the RWA under the revised standardised approaches.
The new floor limits a bank’s RWA to no more than 72.5% of the RWA calculated using only the standardised approaches.
The Basel II floor was set at 80% of Basel I capital requirements and was applied inconsistently across countries; the new floor is based on the revised Basel III standardised approaches.
The new floor applies only to banks using the advanced IRB approach, since banks on the foundation IRB approach already use supervisory LGD and EAD values.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The Basel II floor**

“The Basel II framework introduced an output floor based on Basel I capital requirements. That floor was calibrated at 80% of the relevant Basel I capital requirements.” Its implementation “has been inconsistent across countries”, because of differing interpretations and because it is based on Basel I standards that many banks and jurisdictions no longer apply.

**Step 2 – The Basel III floor**

It is “based on the revised Basel III standardised approaches”: RWA are the higher of RWA under approved approaches and 72.5% of RWA under the standardised approaches only, phased in from 50%.

⇒ C states both halves correctly.

**Interpretation**

This is the C5 S3 comparison: two floors, two bases (Basel I against the revised standardised approaches), two calibrations (80% against 72.5%).

**LO:** ORR-23 c: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor. • **Reference:** BCBS, High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (December 2017), GARP ORR Ch.23, Output Floor and Table 23.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.23 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-23 c.2)

a.reason: The calibrations are swapped: 80% was the Basel II floor on Basel I; 72.5% is the new floor.

b.reason: Polarity flip: it is a floor, not a cap. RWA cannot fall below 72.5% of the standardised-only RWA.

d.reason: Scope error: the floor applies to total RWA of any bank using internal models. F-IRB banks still estimate PD themselves (and market risk models also count), so their modelled RWA can be well below the standardised figure.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.question: A capital manager at a eurozone bank is reporting under the fully phased-in December 2017 framework. The bank’s A-IRB model estimates an LGD of 20% for unsecured loans to corporates with consolidated revenues below EUR 500 million. After all input floors are applied, the bank’s total RWA under its approved approaches is EUR 60 billion; its total RWA calculated using only the standardised approaches is EUR 90 billion. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The modelled LGD is raised to the 25% floor; the output floor does not bind, because EUR 60 billion exceeds 72.5% of the modelled RWA, EUR 43.5 billion.
The modelled LGD is raised to the 25% floor; the output floor binds, because 72.5% of standardised RWA is EUR 65.25 billion, so RWA become EUR 65.25 billion.
The modelled LGD of 20% stands, because LGD floors apply only under F-IRB; the output floor binds, so RWA become EUR 65.25 billion.
The modelled LGD is raised to the 25% floor; the output floor binds, so RWA become EUR 90 billion, the full standardised amount.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Input floor (parameter level)**

Table 23.3: the unsecured corporate LGD floor is 25% under A-IRB. The bank’s 20% estimate is raised to 25% before modelled RWA are computed.

**Step 2 – Output floor (aggregate level)**

$72.5\% \times90 = \text{EUR} 65.25$ billion$, \text{RWA} = \text{max}(60, 65.25) = \text{EUR} 65.25$ billion

⇒ The floor adds EUR 5.25 billion of RWA: the modelled approaches may lower RWA by at most 27.5% relative to the standardised approaches.

**Interpretation**

The two floors act at different levels: input floors constrain individual parameters inside the model; the output floor limits the total benefit of modelling. During the phase-in the floor would bind in 2026 (70% × 90 = 63 > 60) but not in 2025 (65% × 90 = 58.5 \< 60); a supervisor using the transitional cap would limit RWA to 1.25 × 60 = 75, which does not bite here.

**LO:** ORR-23 c: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor. ORR-23 b: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework • **Reference:** BCBS, High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (December 2017), GARP ORR Ch.23, Specification of Input Floors, Output Floor, Transitional Arrangements, Tables 23.3 and 23.5

**Source:** Workbook A31.5 • S5 • self-generated (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-23 c.5)

a.reason: Sibling swap of the base: 72.5% is applied to RWA under the standardised approaches, not to the bank’s own modelled RWA (72.5% × 60 = 43.5).

c.reason: Sibling swap (F-IRB for A-IRB): LGD and EAD floors apply only under A-IRB (under F-IRB, LGD is supervisory anyway).

d.reason: Absolute claim: the floor does not require the full standardised amount; RWA are the higher of modelled RWA and 72.5% of standardised RWA.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.question:
The head of capital management at a eurozone G-SIB is preparing the fully phased-in output floor calculation. The bank’s risk-weighted assets by risk type are (EUR billion):

| Risk type | Approach approved | RWA, approved | RWA, SA only |
|---|---|---|---|
| Credit risk | A-IRB and F-IRB | 480 | 760 |
| Counterparty credit risk | internal model method | 60 | 90 |
| CVA risk | SA-CVA | 30 | 30 |
| Market risk | internal models approach | 62 | 80 |
| Operational risk | standardised approach | 70 | 70 |

The “SA only” column uses the SA for credit risk, SA-CCR exposures with SA risk weights, SA-CVA, the SA for market risk and the SA for operational risk. The bank’s leverage ratio exposure measure is EUR 2,400 billion. Which of the following is closest to the bank’s total RWA after applying the output floor?

options.text: EUR 702.00 billion
EUR 721.00 billion
EUR 746.75 billion
EUR 778.25 billion

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Total RWA under the approved approaches**

$480 + 60 + 30 + 62 + 70 = \text{EUR} 702$ billion

**Step 2 – Total RWA under standardised approaches only**

$760 + 90 + 30 + 80 + 70 = \text{EUR} 1{,}030$ billion

⇒ Every line is recomputed on its standardised approach: SA credit, SA-CCR with SA weights, SA-CVA, SA market risk, SA operational risk.

**Step 3 – Apply the aggregate floor**

$72.5\% \times1{,}030 = 746.75, \text{RWA} = \text{max}(702, 746.75) = \text{EUR} 746.75$ billion

⇒ Modelled RWA are 702/1,030 = 68.2% of the standardised figure, so the floor binds and adds EUR 44.75 billion.

**Interpretation**

The floor is “aggregate”: it compares totals. Applied line by line, each line is floored on its own, which can only give a higher number because a sum of maxima is never below the maximum of the sums. The leverage exposure measure is a red herring: it drives the leverage ratio, not RWA.

**LO:** ORR-23 c: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor. • **Reference:** BCBS, High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (December 2017), GARP ORR Ch.23, Output Floor (approaches to be used); Additional Enhancements (aggregate output floor)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.23 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-23 c.6)

a.reason: Applied 72.5% to the modelled RWA: 72.5% × 702 = 508.95 \< 702, so the floor seems never to bind and RWA stay at 702.

b.reason: Used the 2026 phase-in percentage instead of the fully phased-in 72.5%: max(702, 70% × 1,030) = 721.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.question: A eurozone bank’s supervisor uses the national discretion to cap the increase in risk-weighted assets caused by the output floor during its phase-in. Using the transitional schedule in the Basel Committee’s December 2017 summary (Table 23.5), the bank’s capital manager is computing the RWA that apply from 1 January 2026. The bank’s RWA under its approved approaches are EUR 80 billion, its RWA using only the standardised approaches are EUR 150 billion, and its CET1 capital is EUR 9 billion. Which of the following is closest to the bank’s RWA for 2026?

options.text: EUR 80.00 billion
EUR 100.00 billion
EUR 105.00 billion
EUR 108.75 billion

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Phase-in floor for 2026**

Table 23.5 gives 70% from 1 January 2026:

$70\% \times150 = \text{EUR} 105$ billion$, \text{max}(80, 105) = 105$

⇒ Without the cap the floor would lift RWA by 25, which is 31.25% of the pre-floor RWA.

**Step 2 – Transitional cap**

The increase is capped at 25% of RWA before the floor:

$1.25 \times80 = \text{EUR} 100$ billion

**Step 3 – RWA for 2026**

RWA$_{2026} = \text{min}(105, 100) = \text{EUR} 100$ billion

⇒ The cap binds: RWA rise by EUR 20 billion instead of 25.

**Interpretation**

The CET1 figure is a red herring for the RWA, but it shows the effect: the CET1 ratio falls from 9/80 = 11.25% to 9/100 = 9.00%. The cap is removed on 1 January 2027, when the floor of 72.5% × 150 = 108.75 applies in full.

**LO:** ORR-23 c: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor. • **Reference:** BCBS, High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (December 2017), GARP ORR Ch.23, Output Floor, Transitional Arrangements, Table 23.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.23 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-23 c.7)

a.reason: Treated the cap as switching the floor off: the cap limits the increase to 25%, it does not remove it.

c.reason: Ignored the transitional cap the supervisor has chosen to apply: 70%×150 = 105.

d.reason: Used the fully phased-in 72.5% and no cap: 72.5% × 150 = 108.75, the 2027 figure.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
questions.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.topic: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.question: A compliance analyst is summarising for her bank’s audit committee the regulatory findings in the USAA Federal Savings Bank case of March 2022. Which of the following statements in her summary is correct?

options.text: FinCEN and the Federal Reserve fined the bank after finding that its retail accounts had been used to launder funds for a criminal network over several years.
The deficiencies were confined to a monitoring system introduced in 2021, which generated too few alerts for staff to detect the suspicious activity in time.
The bank admitted that from January 2016 to April 2021 its AML programme failed the BSA minimums, and its understaffed compliance team relied on untrained contractors.
The OCC judged the programme adequate in design; the fine related only to delays in filing suspicious activity reports caused by pandemic-era remote working.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Who fined, and for what**

FinCEN and the OCC, under two separate consent orders, fined USAA FSB USD 140 million in March 2022 for its “willful” failure to implement and maintain a BSA/AML compliance programme.

**Step 2 – Period and admission**

“From January 2016 through April 2021, USAA FSB admitted it failed to implement and maintain an AML program that met the minimum requirements of the BSA.”

**Step 3 – Staffing**

FinCEN: the compliance department was “significantly understaffed”, with shortages supplemented by third-party contractors whom the bank “failed to properly train”.

⇒ C combines the admission and the staﬀing finding.

**Step 4 – The 2021 system**

The new system was “too sensitive” and created an unmanageable number of alerts and cases: about 90,000 unreviewed alerts and 6,900 unreviewed cases by the end of 2021.

**Interpretation**

The findings describe a programme-wide failure over more than five years: controls, suspicious activity reporting, staﬀing, training and third-party risk management. The 2021 system made a long-standing problem worse.

**LO:** ORR-11 b: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.11, Box 11.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-11 b.1)

a.reason: Wrong regulator (the OCC, not the Federal Reserve) and wrong basis: the fine was for control failures, not for proven laundering.

b.reason: Polarity and scope: the system generated too many alerts, and the deficiencies ran from 2016, well before it.

d.reason: The OCC cited inadequate internal controls and risk management practices among other deficiencies; the pandemic point is GARP’s wider context, not a finding against USAA.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
questions.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.topic: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.question: After presenting the USAA case, the CRO of a Singapore bank asks the risk committee which conclusion GARP’s case study supports. Which of the following conclusions is correct?

options.text: Regulatory findings often lead to costly lookbacks, in which the bank reviews all client files for a set period, verifies client data, files suspicious activity reports and may close accounts.
Fines of this kind are a US phenomenon; regulators in the EU, the UK and Asia act only once laundering through a bank has actually been demonstrated.
The use of third-party contractors to clear compliance workloads was itself the breach; banks facing alert backlogs should never use contractors for AML reviews.
The pandemic shift to remote transactions made anomalies easier to identify, because digital channels leave a fuller data trail than branch activity does.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Lookbacks**

“Regulatory findings and sanctions mean costly AML remediation programs, often called lookbacks, in which the bank must review all client files for a specified period, verify client information, file suspicious activity reports … and even close suspicious accounts.”

⇒ A restates GARP.

**Step 2 – Beyond the US**

“Banks in the EU, the UK, and Asia have been fined, sometimes heavily, for being unable to demonstrate that their AML controls have been properly designed and operate effectively.” Asia-Pacific fines reached USD 5.1 billion in 2020, seven times the 2019 level.

**Step 3 – Contractors and the pandemic**

Supplementing staff with contractors “is not unusual in banking”, especially under remediation deadlines; USAA’s failure was not training them. The rise in remote transactions made anomalies harder to identify.

**Interpretation**

The case sits inside a global trend: regulators everywhere fine banks that cannot demonstrate effective controls, and the remediation that follows is often costlier than the fine.

**LO:** ORR-11 b: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.11, Case Study and Box 11.2

ORR-12 • Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-11 b.6)

b.reason: Polarity flip: regulators in the EU, the UK and Asia also fine for undemonstrated controls, without proven laundering.

c.reason: Absolute claim: the use of contractors was not the breach; the lack of training and qualifications was.

d.reason: Polarity flip: remote transactions made anomalies more diﬀicult to identify.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.question: The chief compliance oﬀicer of an Australian wealth manager is briefing the board after a vendor engaged to decommission two client data servers passed the work to a subcontractor, and the hardware was later resold with client data still on it. The firm had not assessed the subcontractor and kept no inventory of the client data held on the servers. The CEO argues that because the master services agreement transferred the decommissioning task, and states that the vendor has overall accountability for its subcontractors, the regulatory exposure now sits with the vendor. Which of the following statements should the CCO include in the briefing?

options.text: Because the agreement gives the vendor overall accountability for its subcontractors, the firm’s own accountability to its clients and its regulator for the breach passes to the vendor.
Outsourcing the decommissioning to a specialist eliminated the operational risk of the activity for the firm, leaving only the vendor’s performance against the contract to be managed.
As decommissioning is infrequent and done by a specialist, lighter oversight than for routine processes was appropriate, so not reviewing the subcontractor was a proportionate choice.
Outsourcing can transfer the task and some of its operational risk, but the board and senior management remain responsible for its safe and lawful conduct; the accountability is not transferable.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the contract can and cannot do**

The subcontracting provision makes the primary provider accountable to the firm for services delivered by its subcontractors. SR 13-19 is explicit that the use of service providers does not relieve the board and senior management of responsibility for safe-and-sound, lawful conduct of the outsourced activity.

⇒ The clause allocates duties between the two companies; it does not move the firm’s accountability to its clients or its regulator.

**Step 2 – Compare with the GARP case**

The facts mirror the Morgan Stanley case: the OCC fined the bank USD 60 million for failing to assess the risks of decommissioning, to assess vendors including subcontractors, and to keep an inventory of customer data stored on the devices. The case’s stated lesson is that outsourcing may transfer some operational risk, but accountability is not transferable.

**Step 3 – What the programme required**

The activity involved sensitive customer information, which puts it squarely inside the risk-focused part of the programme: due diligence that covers subcontractors, contract terms on data security, return and destruction, and monitoring scaled to the risk.

**Interpretation**

D is correct. The CCO should tell the board that the firm owns the breach, must remediate (customer notification, data inventory, subcontractor due diligence standards in vendor contracts), and may pursue the vendor contractually, for example under indemnification, without that changing who answers to the regulator.

**LO:** ORR-12 a: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk. ORR-12 c: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider. ORR-13 a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. ORR-13 b: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies. • **Reference:** Federal Reserve SR 13-19 (GARP ORR Ch.12, 12.3 and 12.4 C, Subcontracting); GARP ORR Ch.13, OCC Fines Morgan Stanley; Ch.5, 5.1 Risk Response

ORR-12 • Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D2.1 • S1 • Map #51 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-12 a.7)

a.reason: Role misassignment: the subcontracting clause makes the vendor accountable to the firm for its subcontractors; it does not transfer the firm’s accountability to clients and regulators, which remains with its board and senior management.

b.reason: Absolute claim: contracting with a third party does not fully mitigate operational risk; it adds third-party risk, and outsourcing is better seen as risk sharing than risk transfer.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the programme is risk-focused on activities that involve sensitive customer information or are critical; such activities call for more rigorous due diligence and monitoring, including of subcontractors, not less.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.question:
A vendor-risk analyst at a Canadian bank is writing up the due diligence on a payments-processing provider and must file three findings under the guidance’s three review areas:

I. The provider has operated for 14 years and has grown its market share for this service every year.

II. Management showed that the provider’s business model can adapt to the market’s shift to real-time payments.

III. The provider’s record-retention schedule and its systems development process were reviewed.

Which filing is consistent with the guidance?

options.text: I: business background, reputation and strategy; II: financial performance and condition; III: operations and internal controls.
I: financial performance and condition; II: business background, reputation and strategy; III: operations and internal controls.
I: financial performance and condition; II: operations and internal controls; III: business background, reputation and strategy.
I: operations and internal controls; II: business background, reputation and strategy; III: financial performance and condition.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Finding I**

Time in business and growth of market share for a given service are the guidance’s examples of the provider’s sustainability, listed under financial performance and condition.

**Step 2 – Finding II**

“The resiliency and adaptability of the service provider’s business model” is assessed as a factor in its future viability under business background, reputation and strategy.

**Step 3 – Finding III**

Maintenance and retention of records, and systems development and maintenance, are on the operations and internal controls list.

⇒ I financial, II strategy, III operations: option B.

**Interpretation**

The trap is that both I and II sound like “staying power”. The guidance splits them: the numbers that show a durable business are financial; whether the model can adapt to change is strategy.

**LO:** ORR-12 b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. • **Reference:** Federal Reserve SR 13-19/CA 13-21 (GARP ORR Ch.12, 12.4 B.1 to B.3)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.12 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-12 b.5)

a.reason: Swaps I and II: sustainability (time in business, market share) is financial; the model’s adaptability is strategy.

c.reason: Puts the business model under operations and record keeping under strategy.

d.reason: Files sustainability under operations and record keeping under financial condition.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.topic: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.question: The head of procurement at a mid-sized U.S. bank proposes to move the printing and mailing of wealth clients’ statements, which carry client names, addresses and balances, to a large print-services firm that the bank has used for years for marketing brochures. Because the bank knows the firm and the firm is a market leader, she suggests signing the contract now and having procurement alone complete a short due diligence questionnaire during onboarding. Which response from the operational risk manager is most consistent with the guidance?

options.text: Familiarity and reputation remove the need for due diligence on this provider; the bank’s effort should go into the indemnification clause of the contract instead.

Familiarity and reputation can reduce the depth and formality of the review, but it must be completed before the bank engages the firm, cover all three review areas, and involve technical experts and key stakeholders, as the service now involves sensitive customer information.
Due diligence can be completed after signing, because ongoing monitoring under the contract will reveal any weakness the review would have found.
As the firm is a market leader, the review need only cover its financial performance and condition; its operations and internal controls are the firm’s own responsibility.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Timing**

The institution should evaluate and perform the necessary due diligence on a prospective provider prior to engaging it.

⇒ Signing first and checking during onboarding is out.

**Step 2 – Depth**

Depth and formality vary with the scope, complexity and importance of the arrangement, the institution’s familiarity with the provider, and its reputation and industry standing. Familiarity and reputation can lighten the review.

**Step 3 – What has changed**

The new service involves sensitive customer information, which the programme treats as a focus area. The review must cover all three areas and draw in technical experts (information security, privacy) and key stakeholders, not procurement alone.

**Interpretation**

The firm is familiar for a low-risk service (brochures); the new arrangement is a different risk. Proportionality is judged on the planned arrangement, not on the vendor’s history with the bank.

**LO:** ORR-12 b: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers. • **Reference:** Federal Reserve SR 13-19/CA 13-21 (GARP ORR Ch.12, 12.4 and 12.4 B)

ORR-12 • Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.12 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-12 b.6)

a.reason: Absolute waiver: familiarity reduces depth, it does not remove the review; an indemnity does not replace due diligence or move accountability.

c.reason: Timing error: due diligence precedes engagement; monitoring is a later, separate element.

d.reason: Partial scope: the review covers all three areas, and the institution is responsible for ensuring the provider’s services comply with laws and safe-and-sound practices.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
questions.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.topic: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.13 and Ch.12
questions.question: An operational risk manager at a Dutch bank is rating its card-authorisation provider, P. The service is critical: card authorisations stop without it. Only two firms in the market offer the service, and the other one, Q, runs its platform from the same data-centre campus as P. P has never had a material outage and its latest SOC 2 report is clean. Which assessment should the manager make?

options.text: Concentration risk is low: P has a clean record and an alternative provider exists, so a standard annual review of P is suﬀicient.

Concentration risk arises from both the few providers and their shared location; P belongs in the highest rating class, and the exit plan must not rely on an alternative with the same point of failure.
Splitting the authorisation volume between P and Q would remove the concentration risk, because the service would no longer depend on a single provider.
Substitutability matters only at the remediation or termination stage, so it should not affect P’s rating while the contract is running.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Identify the risk**

SR 13-19: concentration risk arises when outsourced services are provided by a limited number of providers or are concentrated in limited geographic locations. Both conditions hold: two providers, one campus.

⇒ This is firm-level concentration risk the bank must manage.

**Step 2 – Rate the provider**

On GARP’s rating criteria, process criticality is at the top level (operations halt without the vendor), and substitutability is “none or very limited”: the only alternative fails in the same campus event.

⇒ Highest class: the most frequent and stringent monitoring, a designated point of contact and a tailored mitigation plan.

**Step 3 – The resilience response**

Key-supplier dependency with low substitutability is a single point of failure and a resilience KRI (ORR-4 g). Remove it where possible (a provider or site outside the campus, an in-house fallback for authorisations); otherwise reflect it in impact tolerances and stress tests. Keep a tested continuity plan and an exit strategy with comparable providers that do not share the failure point.

**Interpretation**

A clean SOC 2 report and a clean history describe P’s controls, not the bank’s dependency. The risk sits in the structure: one campus event removes both options at once.

**LO:** ORR-13 a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.13, Figure 13.2 Risk-based vendor rating; Ch.12, 12.2 and 12.4 E and F; Ch.4, 4.5 KRIs for Resilience

ORR-13 • Third-Party Risk Management • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13 and Ch.12 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-13 a.8)

a.reason: Polarity and false comfort: a nominal alternative in the same location does not reduce concentration, and a critical provider gets more monitoring, not a standard review.

c.reason: Half of the definition: dual sourcing answers “a limited number of providers” but not “limited geographic locations”. P and Q run from the same campus, so one campus event still stops every authorisation; the point of failure is shared, not removed.

d.reason: Stage error: substitutability is a rating criterion that sets the intensity of due diligence and monitoring throughout the relationship, not only at exit.

questions.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.topic: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.question: An internal auditor is preparing a slide that pairs each of GARP’s two third-party case studies with the regulator’s penalty and finding. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Capital One: OCC fine of USD 60 million for failing to keep an inventory of customer data stored on decommissioned servers.
Morgan Stanley: OCC fine of USD 80 million after a former cloud-provider employee exploited a misconfigured web application firewall.
Capital One: OCC fine of USD 80 million for failing to establish effective risk assessment processes before migrating significant IT operations to the public cloud.
Morgan Stanley: the penalty was imposed on the decommissioning vendor and its subcontractor, since they handled the hardware that left client data exposed.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Capital One**

OCC, USD 80 million, for “failure to establish effective risk assessment processes prior to migrating significant information technology operations to the public cloud environment”.

⇒ C matches.

**Step 2 – Morgan Stanley**

OCC, USD 60 million, for failing to assess the risks of decommissioning, to assess vendors including subcontractors, and to keep an inventory of customer data on its devices.

**Interpretation**

Two features separate the cases: the technology (cloud configuration against hardware disposal) and the finding (pre-migration risk assessment against vendor oversight and data inventory). Fix those, and the amounts follow.

**LO:** ORR-13 b: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.13, Case Studies

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-13 b.3)

a.reason: Gives Morgan Stanley’s amount and finding to Capital One.

b.reason: Gives Capital One’s amount and circumstances to Morgan Stanley.

d.reason: Role misassignment: the OCC fined the bank; the accountability for vendor oversight stayed with it.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.
questions.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.topic: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.question: A board risk committee asks what the Capital One and Morgan Stanley enforcement actions show about how such penalties arise. Which statement is best supported by the case facts?

options.text: Both penalties followed a single, unforeseeable incident at a well-controlled bank, showing that regulators penalise outcomes rather than control weaknesses.

Both penalties reflected weaknesses that had persisted or recurred: Capital One’s internal audit had earlier failed to identify control gaps in its cloud environment, and Morgan Stanley showed similar decommissioning deficiencies in 2016 and again in 2019.
Neither bank had to remediate with customers, because the data exposure occurred at a third party rather than at the bank itself.
Both penalties were triggered by the banks’ failure to notify customers in time, as the OCC found no deficiency in their risk management.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Capital One’s history**

“Like in other cases of regulatory fines, the bank had a history of weak control environment, and failures to detect or address it, often for years at a time.” The consent order cites an internal audit (2015, four years before the breach) that failed to identify numerous control weaknesses and gaps in the cloud operating environment.

**Step 2 – Morgan Stanley’s history**

Deficiencies in the 2016 decommissioning of two data servers recurred in the 2019 decommissioning of WAAS devices; the OCC’s findings cover both.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Regulators penalise the framework: risk assessment, vendor due diligence and monitoring, data inventories, and the third line’s ability to catch gaps. The incident only makes the weakness visible.

**LO:** ORR-13 b: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.13, Case Studies (Capital One; OCC Fines Morgan Stanley)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-13 b.4)

a.reason: Polarity: both banks had long-standing weaknesses; the penalties targeted control failures.

c.reason: Both banks faced customer remediation and litigation: Morgan Stanley notified customers and offered two years of free credit monitoring and faces a class action; Capital One’s lawsuits were consolidated in 2020.

d.reason: The OCC found deficient risk management (unsafe or unsound practices); notification timing was not the basis of either penalty.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.
questions.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.topic: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.question: A European bank plans to migrate its card-customer database to a public cloud provider. The CIO argues that the provider’s platform has strong built-in security and that the provider is therefore responsible for keeping the data safe. Applying the lessons of the Capital One case, which plan should the CRO require?

options.text: Accept the provider’s built-in security as suﬀicient and focus the bank’s effort on negotiating an indemnity for data breaches.
Complete a risk assessment of the migration before moving the data, configure and use the cloud controls (including encryption of the data), and scan regularly for misconfigurations.
Postpone any review of the cloud configuration to the first annual contract review, since a provider with strong security will flag misconfigurations itself.
Keep the data unencrypted so that the bank’s fraud teams can query it quickly, relying on the web application firewall as the single line of defence.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What Capital One got wrong**

No effective risk assessment before migrating to the public cloud; a misconfigured firewall; data left unencrypted by its own configuration.

**Step 2 – What the case says about cloud providers**

“All the major cloud providers offer the controls needed to keep the data in their cloud buckets private, but customers need to use them.” Risk management, monitoring, back-ups and maintenance remain the business’s responsibility.

**Step 3 – Build the plan**

Assess before migrating; configure and use the controls, with encryption so that stolen data are useless; scan regularly for misconfigurations (Capital One’s own fix after the breach).

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

The CIO’s argument is the one the case refutes. Strong provider security is a capability the bank must use, not a transfer of responsibility.

**LO:** ORR-13 b: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.13, Case Studies, Capital One Data Breach

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-13 b.5)

a.reason: Role misassignment: an indemnity moves some cost, not the accountability, and does nothing to prevent the breach.

c.reason: Timing and polarity: risk assessment must come before migration, and configuration is the customer’s job, not the provider’s.

d.reason: The opposite of the lesson: unencrypted data and a single line of defence are what made the Capital One breach damaging.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
questions.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.topic: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.14 and workbook D21 (MiFID II Art. 25)
questions.question: The head of compliance at a Frankfurt investment firm is checking three retail client files against MiFID II. Client 1 asked the firm’s adviser which structured note to buy for her retirement savings. Client 2, using the firm’s online platform without advice, wants to buy a complex leveraged certificate. Client 3, on his own initiative, placed an order on the platform for shares listed on a regulated market, after being told that the firm would not assess appropriateness. Which description of the firm’s obligations is correct?

options.text: Suitability for all three clients, because all three are retail clients and the test exists to protect retail investors.
Appropriateness for Client 1, since the advice concerns a single product; suitability for Client 2, since the product is complex; no test for Client 3.
Suitability for Client 1; appropriateness for Client 2, with the order refused if the certificate is not appropriate; appropriateness for Client 3.
Suitability for Client 1; appropriateness for Client 2, with a warning if the certificate is not appropriate; no test for Client 3.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Which test goes with which service**

MiFID II (outside the GARP text): suitability for investment advice and portfolio management; appropriateness for other, non-advised services; no test for execution-only dealing in non-complex instruments at the client’s initiative, once the client is told.

**Step 2 – Client by client**

Client 1 receives advice: suitability (knowledge and experience, financial situation including ability to bear losses, objectives including risk tolerance). Client 2 buys a complex product without advice: appropriateness (knowledge and experience only); if it is not appropriate, the firm warns and the client may still proceed. Client 3 buys listed shares, a non-complex instrument, unprompted and informed: execution only.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

The tests scale with the firm’s role. When the firm recommends, it takes on the client’s whole situation; when the client decides, the firm checks only that the client can understand the risks; for a simple product bought unprompted, no test applies. In GARP’s terms this is Basel 4.1 territory, and the same logic condemns incentives that push products regardless of suitability (ORR-12 a, element D).

**LO:** ORR-14 a: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.14, Context and Scope (Basel 4.1); MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU), Art. 25 (outside the GARP text); workbook D21

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14 and workbook D21 (MiFID II Art. 25) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-14 a.7)

a.reason: Over-scope: retail status does not trigger suitability; the service does. Clients 2 and 3 receive no advice.

b.reason: Sibling swap: advice on one product is still advice (suitability), and complexity without advice calls for appropriateness, not suitability.

c.reason: Absolute qualifier and dropped condition: a failed appropriateness test leads to a warning, not a refusal, and Client 3 meets the execution-only conditions.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
questions.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.topic: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.14 and workbook D21 (MiFID II Art. 23, 24)
questions.question: The head of compliance at a Milan bank is reviewing its private bank against the MiFID II and MiFIR conflicts-of-interest rules. The bank markets its advice as independent. Relationship managers earn a bonus tied to sales of the bank’s own funds, the bank keeps trail commissions (retrocessions) paid by third-party fund houses whose funds it recommends, and the proprietary trading desk sits next to the client execution desk with no separation. Which plan is consistent with the rules?

options.text: Keep all three arrangements and disclose each of them in detail to every client, since disclosure is the primary tool for managing conflicts.
Stop retaining the retrocessions on independent advice, stop rewarding staff for selling the bank’s own funds over better-suited ones, separate the proprietary desk, and disclose only what remains.
Keep the retrocessions, since fund houses rather than clients pay them, and fix only the bonus scheme and the separation of the two desks.
Leave the bonus scheme unchanged, since staff remuneration is governed by employment law and falls outside the scope of MiFID II and MiFIR.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the package targets**

GARP: MiFID II and MiFIR address the remuneration of traders and advisors and conflicts of interest, and the definition and independence of investment advice. Traders who deal for clients and for the firm’s own book are a named driver of compliance risk.

**Step 2 – Independent advice**

Outside the GARP text (MiFID II, Art. 24): a firm that calls its advice independent must not accept and retain third-party fees or commissions; any it receives go to the client in full. The retrocessions must stop being retained.

**Step 3 – Remuneration and the desks**

Staff must not be paid or assessed in a way that rewards recommending one product when another would better meet the client’s needs: redesign the bonus. The desk conflict is prevented or managed by organisational separation (information barriers, separate supervision).

**Step 4 – Then disclose**

Disclosure is the last resort, for whatever the arrangements cannot prevent with reasonable confidence.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

The order is identify, prevent or manage, and only then disclose. Disclosure cannot legitimise a banned practice (inducements in independent advice) or replace sound pay design.

**LO:** ORR-14 a: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.14, Evolution in Recent Years: MIFID II; Compliance Risk Management in Investment Activities; MiFID II, Art. 23 and 24 (outside the GARP text)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14 and workbook D21 (MiFID II Art. 23, 24) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-14 a.8)

a.reason: Sequence error: disclosure is the last resort, not the primary tool, and it cannot cure retrocessions on advice sold as independent.

c.reason: The conflict arises precisely because the fund house pays: the payment rewards recommending its funds. Retrocessions are the inducements the independence rule targets.

d.reason: Scope error: GARP lists the remuneration of traders and advisors among the items the MiFID II/MiFIR package addresses.

questions.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.

questions.topic: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.14 and workbook D21 (Volcker exemptions)
questions.question: A trainee in the Volcker compliance team of a U.S. bank holding company drafts four notes for the bank’s trading manual. Which note is correct?

options.text: The rule bars the bank from all trading for its own account, including market making for clients and hedging of its own positions.
The bond desk qualifies for the market-making exemption whenever it quotes two-way prices, however large its inventory is relative to client demand.
The rule limits proprietary trading by any fund manager, so the hedge funds in which the bank invests must also stop trading for profit.
Market-making inventory must be designed not to exceed clients’ reasonably expected near-term demand, and hedges must target specific, identifiable risks of the bank’s positions.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The prohibition**

GARP: the Volcker Rule intends to prevent commercial banks from speculative activities and proprietary trading for profit, and limits their investments in hedge funds and private equity funds.

**Step 2 – The exemptions**

Outside the GARP text (implementing regulations, 2013): market making is permitted if inventory is designed not to exceed the reasonably expected near-term demand of clients, customers or counterparties; risk-mitigating hedging is permitted if designed to reduce specific, identifiable risks of the bank’s positions. Underwriting, government obligations and trading on behalf of customers are also permitted.

**Step 3 – Test each note**

A drops the exemptions; B drops the demand condition; C extends the rule beyond banks. D states both conditions.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

Scope and condition errors are the natural distractors. The rule targets a purpose, profit from the bank’s own positions, so a permitted activity turns into prohibited proprietary trading when its condition fails: inventory beyond client demand, or a “hedge” tied to no identifiable risk.

**LO:** ORR-14 a: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including MiFiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.14, The Investor Protection Act - Dodd-Frank (Volcker Rule); Volcker Rule implementing regulations, 2013 (outside the GARP text); workbook D21

ORR-14 • Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14 and workbook D21 (Volcker exemptions) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-14 a.9)

a.reason: Scope error: market making for clients and risk-mitigating hedging are permitted activities.

b.reason: Dropped condition: quoting two-way prices is not enough; inventory beyond expected near-term client demand is proprietary trading.

c.reason: Scope error: the rule binds banking entities; it limits the bank’s stake in covered funds (broadly 3% of any one fund and 3% of Tier 1 capital in aggregate), not the funds’ own trading.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
questions.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.topic: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.question: A trading-surveillance analyst at a commodities broker flags a trader who repeatedly places large sell orders in gold futures, cancels them within seconds before they can be filled, and buys at the lower prices that follow. Drawing on GARP’s JP Morgan case, which assessment is correct?

options.text: The pattern is legitimate liquidity provision, because cancelled orders never execute and so cannot move prices or harm other investors.
The pattern is spoofing, but it is a matter for the broker’s internal policy rather than for regulators, since none of the broker’s clients was directly harmed.
The pattern is spoofing, a false impression of market demand created by rapidly entering and cancelling orders; JP Morgan paid USD 920 million to the CFTC for such conduct.
The pattern was a violation only before investor protection rules were modernised; today’s rules accept rapid order cancellation as normal market practice.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Name the pattern**

Orders placed with no intention of execution, cancelled within seconds, and a trade on the price move they caused: spoofing, “providing a false impression of market demand by rapidly entering and canceling orders and therefore manipulating prices in one’s favor”.

**Step 2 – The GARP case**

JP Morgan holds the record spoofing fine: USD 920 million, imposed by the CFTC in September 2020, for spoofing in precious metals and U.S. Treasury markets over at least eight years, with hundreds of thousands of spoof orders.

⇒ C.

**Step 3 – The lesson**

Before investor protection regulation, practices like spoofing were accepted as normal; they are now violations that draw large fines.

**Interpretation**

Spoofing harms everyone who trades at the manipulated prices, not only the firm’s own clients, which is why it is an investor protection violation (Basel 4.2, Improper Business or Market Practices). Being intentional, it is also a form of internal fraud for control purposes, and an eight-year pattern points to weak supervision of trades.

**LO:** ORR-14 b: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.14, Statistics and Record Fines Cases for Investor Protection Violations (JP Morgan)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-14 b.3)

a.reason: The cancelled orders are the manipulation: they move prices without ever being meant to execute.

b.reason: Scope error: spoofing violates investor protection law and draws regulatory fines whoever the counterparties are.

d.reason: Polarity flip of the lesson: practices once accepted as normal became violations, not the reverse.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
questions.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.topic: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.question: A compliance trainer is building a table of GARP’s three investor protection cases. Which row is correct?

options.text: UBS (2008): CFTC fine of USD 920 million for spoofing in precious metals markets.
JP Morgan (2020): FINRA fine of USD 2 million for routing customer orders through the SuperX ping.
Deutsche Bank Securities (2022): USD 11.15 billion resolution for misrepresenting auction rate securities as cash equivalents.
Deutsche Bank Securities (2022): FINRA fine of USD 2 million for best execution failures between 2014 and 2018.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – UBS**

July 2008; USD 11.15 billion resolution of multi-state litigation over auction rate securities sold as safe, cash-equivalent products.

**Step 2 – JP Morgan**

CFTC; USD 920 million; September 2020; spoofing in precious metals and Treasuries.

**Step 3 – Deutsche Bank Securities**

FINRA; USD 2 million (2022); best execution failures from 2014 to 2018.

⇒ Only D matches.

**Interpretation**

Three anchors separate the cases: the conduct (auction rate securities, spoofing, order routing), the authority (multi-state litigation, CFTC, FINRA) and the scale (billions, hundreds of millions, a few million).

**LO:** ORR-14 b: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.14, Case Studies

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-14 b.4)

a.reason: Gives JP Morgan’s regulator, amount and conduct to UBS.

b.reason: Gives Deutsche Bank Securities’ regulator, amount and conduct to JP Morgan.

c.reason: Gives UBS’s resolution and conduct to Deutsche Bank Securities.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
questions.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.topic: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.question: During a spike in market volatility, two compliance breaches occur at a broker-dealer. In the first, an overloaded middle-oﬀice clerk applies an outdated client-classification policy and books several clients into products they should not have been offered. In the second, a trader deliberately buys ahead of a large client order on the firm’s own book. Which statement about classifying and controlling these breaches is correct?

options.text: Both breaches are internal fraud, because any breach of investor protection rules is an unauthorised activity.
Both breaches are human errors, because volatility spikes raise transaction volumes and the frequency of mistakes.
The first is an unintentional breach and the second is internal fraud; most internal fraud controls help against both, but deterrent controls work only against the second.
The second breach can be prevented only by deterrent controls such as sanctions, while monitoring and supervision of trades address only errors.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The first breach**

No intention: an overloaded clerk and an outdated policy. GARP: unintentional compliance breaches are often due to human error or faulty policies.

**Step 2 – The second breach**

A deliberate trade ahead of a client order on the firm’s own book: an intentional breach, a form of internal fraud because it is an unauthorised activity. It is driven by the conflict of traders who trade both for clients and for the firm’s own book.

**Step 3 – The controls**

Many controls against internal fraud also prevent errors (monitoring and supervision of employees and trades, middle and back oﬀice, policies, training, ethics culture), with the exception of deterrent controls, because the key difference between an error and a fraud is intention.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The volatility spike drives both breaches (more transactions, more errors, abnormal trades easier to hide), but it does not decide the classification; intention does.

**LO:** ORR-14 b: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.14, Compliance Risk Management in Investment Activities

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-14 b.5)

a.reason: Sibling swap: only intentional breaches are internal fraud; unintentional ones come from human error or faulty policies.

b.reason: Driver confused with classification: volatility raises the frequency of errors, but the second breach was deliberate.

d.reason: Reversed: monitoring and supervision of trades are core controls against fraud as well as errors; deterrent controls are the one group that does not help against errors.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
questions.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.topic: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
questions.question: The head of execution quality at a U.S. broker-dealer is reviewing its equity order routing. Customer market orders go first to an aﬀiliated venue for a “ping” before any part reaches an exchange, unless the customer opts out. Internal data show that pinged orders execute more slowly and fill less often than orders sent straight to exchanges. The firm earns trading rebates from some venues, which its reports mention only as rebates it “may receive”. Drawing on FINRA’s Deutsche Bank Securities case, which response best meets the firm’s best execution obligation?

options.text: Compare execution quality with direct exchange routing, change the routing if speed, fill rates or price improvement are worse, and disclose the rebates in detail.
Keep the routing, since customers who prefer direct routing can opt out, and offering an opt-out shifts the best execution duty to the customer.
Keep the routing as long as pinged orders receive the same price as direct routing, since best execution is judged on price alone.
Keep the routing but pass all rebates on to customers, since passing rebates on is by itself enough to satisfy the best execution obligation.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The obligation**

FINRA Rule 5310: seek the most favourable terms reasonably available for a customer’s order; the criteria include price improvement and speed of execution.

**Step 2 – Match the facts**

A ping before any part reaches an exchange unless the customer opts out, slower execution, lower fill rates, rebates mentioned only vaguely: the Deutsche Bank Securities pattern.

**Step 3 – What the case says was missing**

Changing the routing once its effects were known; evaluating the price improvement available from direct exchange routing; disclosing rebate details (amount per share or per order) and whether customers receive them.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

Outside the GARP text, FINRA expects firms that route orders to review execution quality regularly and rigorously against other venues; MiFID II’s best execution weighs price, costs, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, size and nature of the order. Both point to the same remedy.

**LO:** ORR-14 b: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations. • **Reference:** GARP ORR Ch.14, FINRA Fines Deutsche Bank Securities, Inc. \$2 Million for Best Execution Violations; workbook D21

ORR-15 • Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-14 b.7)

b.reason: Role misassignment: Deutsche Bank Securities’ customers could also opt out, and FINRA still fined the firm; the duty stays with the broker.

c.reason: Scope error: speed of execution and fill rates are part of best execution, not price alone.

d.reason: Partial fix: passing rebates on answers the disclosure finding, but slower execution and lower fill rates remain a best execution failure.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
questions.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.question: A market risk team at a European bank built a full-revaluation VaR model whose theory and code were approved by validation. To meet the overnight batch window, IT re-implements it in the production risk engine, replacing full revaluation of the options book with a delta-gamma approximation and sourcing positions from a new data warehouse. The VaR output also feeds the bank’s economic capital model and its limit-setting model. Which of the following statements about the model risk this creates is correct?

options.text: Because the theory and code were approved before the change, errors introduced when the model is re-coded into the production engine are IT risk, not model risk.
Model risk is assessed one model at a time, so the capital and limit models that take the VaR as an input carry no extra model risk from the change.
Model risk falls as the VaR output is used more widely across the bank, because broader use exposes errors faster and reduces uncertainty about the model.
The approximation and the new data source can compromise the output even though the theory is sound, and the effect can spread to every model that uses the VaR.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where errors can enter**

GARP’s chain runs from theory through sample design and numerical routines, inputs and estimation, to implementation in information systems, and “errors can occur at any point from design through implementation”. Shortcuts, simplifications or approximations “could compromise the integrity and reliability of outputs”, and output quality depends on input data.

⇒ The delta-gamma shortcut and the new position feed are both implementation-stage sources of model risk.

**Step 2 – Size and aggregation**

Model risk increases with complexity, uncertain inputs, broader use and larger impact, and must be assessed individually and in aggregate. Aggregate model risk rises with dependencies among models and reliance on common data or assumptions.

⇒ Two downstream models now inherit any VaR error.

**Interpretation**

A change in technique of this kind is a material change: it should be validated before it goes into production, and process verification (code, data, systems integration) should follow it in ongoing monitoring (ORR-15 d).

**LO:** ORR-15 a: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model. • **Reference:** FDIC FIL-22-2017 (GARP ORR Ch.15), 15.3 and 15.4 (Model Development and Implementation)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-15 a.5)

a.reason: Scope error. Implementation in information systems is part of the model calculation; errors there are model risk, whatever the earlier approval.

b.reason: Ignores aggregate model risk, which arises precisely from dependencies among models and shared inputs.

c.reason: Polarity flip. Model risk increases with broader use and larger potential impact.

questions.question: A credit risk consultant is presenting to newly hired analysts at a Japanese trust bank on lessons from the 2007 to 2009 crisis. One slide maps the subprime securitisation chain as a series of frictions between pairs of parties, and labels the friction between CDO investors and the credit rating agencies as model error. An analyst asks how that label connects to the GARP case study on Gaussian copula pricing of CDOs. Which of the following statements should the consultant give as correct?

options.text: Investors relied on ratings and prices from a Gaussian copula calibrated to a short, benign CDS history; when correlations spiked the assumption failed, yet users kept relying on outputs whose limitations they did not understand.
The friction is an execution error: like the hidden rows in the Barclays spreadsheet, the copula failed to do what it was designed to do, so replicating its code would have exposed the problem.
The friction would have been removed by a suﬀiciently rigorous validation of the copula before use, because robust validation of a sound model eliminates its model risk.
The copula produced inaccurate CDO prices in all market conditions, so the losses came from a fundamental flaw in Li’s formula rather than from how users relied on it.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Name the friction**

In the securitisation-frictions taxonomy, the investor depends on the rating agency’s model to judge the credit quality of the tranche it buys; the friction is that the model can be wrong or wrongly used, hence “model error” (outside-source framing).

⇒ The investor’s risk sits inside someone else’s model, and it is model risk in the ORR-15 sense: adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs.

**Step 2 – Map it to the GARP case**

Li’s Gaussian copula inferred correlation from CDS prices. CDSs had only about a decade of history in a benign period, so implied correlations were very low and sensitive to house prices. The method was adopted by investors, banks, rating agencies and regulators. It worked in normal conditions; when house prices reversed, implied correlations shot up, and banks kept pricing with the old assumptions.

⇒ This is a conceptual error (an assumption that held only in one context) combined with misuse (blind reliance on a black box).

**Step 3 – The MRM lesson**

MRM must replicate the model to rule out coding errors, but its more critical job is to challenge assumptions and explain limitations to non-quantitative users in plain terms.

**Interpretation**

The investor and rating agency friction is model risk of the conceptual-and-misuse type, exactly the failure in the Gaussian copula case, and the remedy is transparency about assumptions, not just better code.

**LO:** ORR-16 a: Define a model and describe different ways that financial institutions can become exposed to model risk. ORR-16 c: Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk. ORR-15 a: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.16, Model Risks and Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing; Ch.15, 15.3

ORR-15 • Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook C6.1 • S1 • Map #32 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-15 a.6)

b.reason: Sibling swap (case cross-mapping): execution error and the Barclays hidden-rows lesson describe an implementation failure in a tool that is not even a model; the copula did what it was designed to do, on an assumption that stopped holding.

c.reason: Absolute claim: even with skilled modelling and robust validation, model risk cannot be eliminated; other tools (limits on use, monitoring, revision, supplementary analysis) are still needed.

d.reason: Scope/condition error: the copula assumption was valid and accurate in normal market conditions; dropping that condition also reverses the case’s verdict that the problem was not the formula itself but its blind use without updating correlations.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
questions.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
questions.question: The head of model risk at a Singapore bank is drafting the charter of a newly created model risk management (MRM) function. The charter is organised around the three elements named in the supervisory guidance: model development, implementation and use; model validation; and governance, policies and controls. The validation team has four staff and the bank runs over 300 models, so some testing of lower-tier models is currently performed by the model developers. Which of the following statements is appropriate to include in the charter?

options.text: Model owners in the business units, who carry ultimate accountability for model use and performance, should hold the authority to restrict a model’s use once validation finds significant deficiencies.
To preserve independence, no validation work may be performed by developers or users, and any testing they have already done must be discarded and repeated in full by the MRM team.
Incentives for effective challenge are strongest when validators sit close to the development process, because that proximity is what gives them the competence to critique a model.

Developers may perform some validation work if an independent party critically reviews it and adds further testing; independence may be supported by reporting lines but is judged by actions and outcomes.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Place the problem in the three components**

Development, implementation and use (first line: developers and model owners); validation (independent effective challenge); governance, policies and controls (board, senior management, policies, roles, inventory, documentation, internal audit). The staﬀing gap sits in the second component, but the cure is written into the third.

**Step 2 – What independence requires**

Validation is generally done by people not responsible for development or use. As a practical matter some validation work may be done most effectively by developers and users, provided it is subject to critical review by an independent party who conducts additional activities. Independence may be supported by separate reporting lines but should be judged by actions and outcomes.

⇒ The charter can keep developer testing on lower-tier models, but only with independent review on top, and must evidence independence through results (models changed after validation).

**Step 3 – Effective challenge**

It needs incentives (stronger with greater separation from development, plus compensation and culture), competence, and influence (authority, stature, senior support).

**Interpretation**

D is the guidance’s own answer to scarce validation resources, combined with tiering so that the full-scope effort goes to the highest-tier models.

**LO:** ORR-15 b: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process. ORR-15 d: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process. ORR-16 b: Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.15, 15.3 and 15.5 (Model Validation), 15.6 (Roles and Responsibilities); Ch.16, Model Risk Management

ORR-15 • Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook C6.2 • S2, S3 • Map #32 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-15 b.6)

a.reason: Role misassignment: the model owner is accountable for use and performance, but the authority to restrict the use of models belongs to risk-control staff, whose temporary exceptions are themselves subject to other controls.

b.reason: Absolute claim: the guidance expressly allows some validation work by developers and users if an independent party critically reviews it; a blanket ban and full repetition is not required.

c.reason: Polarity flip: incentives to provide effective challenge are stronger when there is greater separation of that challenge from the model development process; competence comes from technical skill and business familiarity, not proximity.

questions.topic: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management

questions.question: The head of internal audit at a US regional bank is assessing the bank’s model validation unit. The unit reports to the CRO, separately from all model developers. Its staff hold advanced quantitative degrees and have worked in the business lines whose models they review, and their bonuses are tied to the quality of their validation reports. However, over the past three years the unit has logged a long list of findings on high-tier models, none of which has led to a model being changed or its use restricted. The unit head has no authority to escalate findings to the risk committee, and the unit ranks below the model owners in the bank’s hierarchy. Which conclusion should internal audit draw?

options.text: Effective challenge is weakest on incentives, so validators’ bonuses should instead be linked to the number of models they approve each year.
Effective challenge is weakest on influence, so the unit needs explicit authority to elevate findings and the stature to get issues addressed, shown by models actually changed.
Effective challenge is weakest on competence, so the validators need further technical training before model owners can be expected to act on their findings.
Effective challenge is weakest on independence, so validators should be embedded in the development teams, where their findings would be acted upon faster.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The three ingredients**

Validation “should be performed by staff with appropriate incentives, competence, and influence.”

**Step 2 – Test each against the facts**

Incentives: the unit reports separately from developers and is paid on the quality of its work, so present. Competence: advanced degrees and business-line experience, so present. Influence: no authority to escalate, rank below the owners, and no model ever changed, so missing.

⇒ Influence is the gap.

**Step 3 – What influence requires**

Explicit authority “to challenge developers and users and to elevate their findings”; reporting to someone with “suﬀicient influence or stature”; reflected in “reporting lines, title, rank, or designated responsibilities”; and “demonstrated by a pattern of actual instances in which models… have been appropriately changed as a result of validation”.

**Interpretation**

The evidence of failure is the outcome: findings with no consequences. GARP judges independence the same way, “by actions and outcomes”. Evaluating the objectivity, competence and organisational standing of validators is exactly internal audit’s task.

**LO:** ORR-15 d: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.

- **Reference:** FDIC FIL-22-2017 (GARP ORR Ch.15), 15.3 and 15.5 Model Validation; 15.6 Internal Audit

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15 • S3 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-15 d.8)

a.reason: Polarity flip on incentives: compensation should be tied to the quality of validations and the degree of critical, unbiased review; paying for approvals rewards bias.

c.reason: Competence is already present; more training does not give the unit authority.

d.reason: Polarity flip: incentives for challenge are stronger with greater separation from development; embedding validators removes independence.
