questions.question: At a budget meeting of a mid-sized bank, the CFO proposes halving the model risk management (MRM) budget. Her argument: over the past five years MRM has found many model errors, but none of them would have caused a material loss, so the bank’s model risk is evidently small. The CRO is asked to respond. Which response is most consistent with the GARP case study on model risk?

options.text: Agree: a five-year record in which every error found was benign is good evidence that the bank’s model risk is low, so the MRM budget can follow the loss record.
Agree in part: keep challenging conceptual assumptions but stop checking for coding and data errors, since execution errors are trivial and cannot cause a material loss.
Disagree only for regulatory capital models: other models cannot produce losses large enough to concern shareholders or regulators, so their review can be cut.
Disagree: model risk is a tail risk; most errors are benign or caught early, while large losses come rarely, under extreme conditions and often from a series of mistakes.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Model risk is a tail risk**

“Most errors are benign and are either caught early enough or do not lead to material losses. This often leaves institutions with misplaced confidence in their ability to manage the risk.”

⇒ Five benign years are what a tail risk looks like most of the time.

**Step 2 – How the large losses arrive**

“The tail risks typically materialize under extreme conditions and often involve a series of mistakes in the development, deployment, and use of models.”

**Step 3 – Why the budget looks too big**

The rarity of such events “makes the cost of modern model risk functions seem disproportionate relative to the risk”, because management’s horizons rarely align with the risk or with those of shareholders and regulators.

⇒ The CRO should disagree, for the reason in D.

**Interpretation**

The CFO’s argument is the misplaced confidence GARP describes. The NASA case adds that it is impossible to tell in advance which benign-looking mistakes will turn out to be catastrophic (ORR-16 c).

**LO:** ORR-16 a: Define a model and describe different ways that financial institutions can become exposed to model risk. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.16, Definition and History; 2. Model Risks; NASA Mars Orbiter

ORR-16 • Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.16 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-16 a.6)

a.reason: Treats the absence of tail losses over a short window as evidence that the tail is thin: exactly the misplaced confidence GARP warns about.

b.reason: Execution errors “often seem like trivial errors that cannot result in a material loss”, yet with bad luck they have caused catastrophic ones (Barclays, NASA).

c.reason: Losses are not confined to regulatory models; tiering (ORR-16 b) also weighs materiality, complexity and client-facing use, and lower tiers are reviewed less often, not dropped.

questions.reading: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
questions.topic: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.16 • S3
questions.question: The newly appointed head of model risk management at a US bank that runs several hundred models presents a reorganisation plan to the board risk committee. The second-line validation team is to be doubled in size. Which element of the plan is consistent with the best practices described in the GARP case study?

options.text: Embed each validator within a model development team, so that validators gain the detailed model knowledge they need to challenge models effectively.
Let modeling teams scale back their own quality assurance, because the enlarged second-line team now exists to catch the errors the first line misses.
Validate every model in full each year, whatever its tier, so that model risk management becomes a continuous rather than a point-in-time exercise.
Tier models by materiality, complexity, client-facing use and regulatory use, with full-scope validation of top-tier models about every 2 to 3 years and an annual review of every model.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Tiering**

Tier criteria: materiality of output, complexity, client-facing use, regulatory use. Top tier: full-scope validation “usually every 2 to 3 years”; mid tier every 4 or 5; low tier more rarely; “all models, independently of their tier, undergo an annual review”.

⇒ D is GARP’s practice.

**Step 2 – Independence and the first line**

MRM’s experts are “independent of model development”. A bigger second line “can result in modeling teams becoming more complacent”; the first line owns the risk and its QA/QC teams target execution risk.

⇒ A and B break the independence and ownership rules.

**Step 3 – What “continuous” means**

Continuous model risk management means monitoring and review between validations (owners’ monitoring reports, annual reviews), not full-scope validation of everything every year.

**Interpretation**

The plan’s one sound element spends a scarce validation budget where the risk is. The two independence traps (A and B) are the S3 shape: separation from development drives the incentive to challenge, and the backstop must not let the first line off the hook.

**LO:** ORR-16 b: Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes. ORR-15 d: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.16, 3. Model Risk Management; Ch.15, 15.3 and 15.5

ORR-16 • Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.16 • S3 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-16 b.6)

a.reason: Polarity flip: incentives for effective challenge are stronger with greater separation from development; embedding validators removes the independence that defines MRM.

b.reason: The first line must not abdicate its responsibilities; this is exactly the complacency GARP warns a large validation team can cause.

c.reason: Ignores tiering and the cost-benefit balance; every model gets an annual review, not an annual full-scope validation.

questions.reading: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
questions.topic: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.16 and workbook C6 notes • S1
questions.question: A credit risk consultant running a model risk workshop maps the subprime securitisation chain as a set of frictions between pairs of parties (the Ashcraft and Schuermann taxonomy). She asks the class to label the friction between CDO investors and the credit rating agencies, and to state the lesson the GARP Gaussian copula case attaches to it. Which answer should the class give?

options.text: Principal-agent problem: the investor delegates credit analysis to the agency, so the lesson is to align the agency’s fees with the investor’s returns.
Moral hazard: the agency stops monitoring the collateral once the deal closes, so the lesson is that investors must audit the agency’s surveillance.
Model error: investors relied on rating models built on correlations inferred from a short, benign CDS history, so assumptions and limitations must be challenged and explained.
Adverse selection: the agency knows more about the collateral than the investor, so the lesson is that investors should hold only the most senior tranches.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The label**

In the securitisation-frictions taxonomy the investor relies on the rating agency’s model to judge the credit quality of a tranche, so that friction is labelled model error.

**Step 2 – The GARP case behind it**

Li’s copula, with correlations inferred from a short, benign CDS history, was adopted by “ratings agencies” among others. When house prices reversed, the implied correlations shot up and users kept pricing on the old assumptions.

⇒ The lesson: challenge the assumptions and make sure users understand the limitations.

**Interpretation**

This is the recall item: the exam named the investor and rating agency pair, and the answer was model error. The GARP chapter does not use the frictions taxonomy; the label comes from the outside source in the workbook notes, and the copula case supplies the content.

**LO:** ORR-16 c: Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk. ORR-16 a: Define a model and describe different ways that financial institutions can become exposed to model risk. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.16, Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing; workbook C6 revision notes (Ashcraft and Schuermann, 2008)

ORR-23 • High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.16 and workbook C6 notes • S1 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-16 c.7)

a.reason: Principal-agent is the friction between the asset manager and the investor.

b.reason: Moral hazard is the servicer’s friction (with the mortgagor or with third parties).

d.reason: Adverse selection is the friction between the arranger and third parties.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.question: The CRO of an Australian bank asks a regulatory analyst to explain to the board which shortcomings the December 2017 Basel III reforms were designed to fix. Which of the following pairings of a shortcoming with the reform that addresses it is correct?

options.text: CVA losses were small relative to default losses in the crisis, so the internal CVA model was retained and the standardised approach removed.
The Basel II floor was applied too conservatively across countries, so it was replaced by a lower floor of 72.5% of Basel I requirements.
IRB capital requirements were too uniform across banks, so the reforms gave banks more freedom to estimate LGD and EAD for large corporates.
Operational risk capital proved insuﬀicient for some banks’ losses, and misconduct losses were hard to model, so the AMA was replaced by a single standardised approach.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The operational risk motivation**

GARP: “capital requirements for operational risk proved insuﬀicient to cover operational risk losses incurred by some banks”, and the nature of the losses (misconduct, inadequate systems and controls) “highlighted the diﬀiculty associated with using internal models”. The AMA and the three standardised approaches are replaced by a single standardised approach.

⇒ D pairs the right shortcoming with the right reform.

**Step 2 – Test the other pairings**

CVA losses were large (in some instances above default losses), and the CVA internal model was removed. The Basel II floor was applied inconsistently, not too conservatively, and the new floor is on the revised standardised approaches. IRB requirements lacked comparability, and A-IRB was removed for large corporates.

**Interpretation**

Every motivation in the chapter points the same way: models had produced capital that was too low or too dispersed, so the reforms tightened them.

**LO:** ORR-23 a: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework. • **Reference:** BCBS, High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (December 2017), GARP ORR Ch.23, IRB, CVA, Operational Risk Framework, Output Floor

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.23 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-23 a.6)

a.reason: Both halves reversed: CVA losses were a major source of crisis losses, and the internal model was removed, leaving SA-CVA and BA-CVA.

b.reason: Wrong shortcoming and wrong base: the Basel II floor was inconsistently implemented and based on Basel I; the new floor is 72.5% of RWA under the revised standardised approaches.

c.reason: Reversed: the problem was lack of comparability, and the reforms took the A-IRB away from large corporates (F-IRB fixes LGD and EAD).

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.
questions.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.topic: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
questions.question: A regulatory consultant is briefing the credit risk committee of a European bank that currently uses the Advanced IRB approach for its wholesale, specialised lending and equity exposures. The committee wants to know how the December 2017 Basel III reforms change the bank’s use of internal ratings. Which of the following statements should the consultant include?

options.text: Exposures to corporates with consolidated revenues above EUR 500 million must move to the standardised approach, since the advanced IRB option is removed for them.
Equity exposures can no longer be treated under any IRB approach, whereas specialised lending may remain on the advanced or foundation IRB approach.
Exposures to banks and other financial institutions may stay on the advanced IRB approach, since only corporate exposures lose the advanced option.
PD input floors apply only under the advanced IRB approach, so exposures moved to the foundation IRB approach face no PD floor.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the reform targets**

The Committee removed the A-IRB option “for asset classes that cannot be modelled in a robust and prudent manner”, adopted input floors, and specified estimation practices more tightly, to reduce complexity and unwarranted RWA variability (ORR-23 a).

**Step 2 – Table 23.2, revised scope**

Large and mid-sized corporates (revenues above EUR 500 million): F-IRB or SA. Banks and other financial institutions: F-IRB or SA. Equities: SA only. Specialised lending: A-IRB, F-IRB, slotting or SA.

**Interpretation**

B is the only statement consistent with Table 23.2: “all IRB approaches are being removed for exposures to equities, which are typically a small component of the credit risk of banks”, while banks “would be permitted to continue using the advanced and foundation IRB approaches” for specialised lending.

**LO:** ORR-23 b: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework. ORR-23 a: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.

- **Reference:** BCBS, High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (December 2017), GARP ORR Ch.23, Internal Ratings-Based Approaches for Credit Risk, Tables 23.2 and 23.3

**Source:** Workbook A31.4 • S4 • self-generated (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-23 a.7)

a.reason: Scope error. Losing A-IRB does not mean losing IRB: banks with supervisory approval use F-IRB for these corporates, which fixes LGD and EAD and so removes two sources of RWA variability.

c.reason: Sibling swap. Banks and other financial institutions are in the same position as large corporates: A-IRB is removed for both.

d.reason: Sibling swap. The LGD and EAD floors are A-IRB only; the PD floors apply under both F-IRB and A-IRB (5 bp for corporates).

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
questions.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.topic: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.question: A risk and control self-assessment (RCSA) workshop at a European asset manager has rated two risks above appetite. The second-line facilitator is drafting the follow-up memo. Which of the following statements is correct for the memo?

options.text: The action plans should be owned by the operational risk function that ran the workshop, because the business line is not independent of its own risks.
A risk rated “1-in-10-year” should be read as expected about once over ten years, so a ten-year horizon suits its assessment.
The action plans should be owned by the business-line managers who sign off the results and tracked by the second or third line; mitigation need not mean new controls.
Financial impacts should be rated in absolute currency amounts, so that the same loss receives the same rating in every department of the firm.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Who owns the outcome**

Results are submitted to business-line managers for approval and sign-off; they are responsible for the output and for the action plans. “It is crucial for action plans to be owned by the first line (business-line managers) rather than the second line”; plans are “tracked and reported by the second line or the third line”.

**Step 2 – What mitigation can be**

“Risk mitigation does not necessarily mean adding controls”: reduce volumes, limit access rights, redesign controls, buy insurance.

⇒ C combines both points.

**Interpretation**

Ownership by the business creates the incentive to deliver; the risk function’s role is to facilitate, challenge and track.

**LO:** ORR-4 b: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.4, 4.2 Severity Assessment, Likelihood Assessment Scales, Outcome of RCSAs

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.4 (4.2) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-4 b.3)

a.reason: Role misassignment: the second line facilitates and tracks; the first line owns.

b.reason: Scope error: a 1-in-10-year event has a 10% chance within the next year; RCSA horizons are one year at most.

d.reason: Relative scales (percent of revenue or operating income) make one definition fit departments of different sizes; an absolute amount significant for one unit is minor for another.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
questions.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.topic: Risk Measurement and Assessment
questions.question: The head of operational risk at a custody bank reviews the monthly dashboard and sees that the number of trade confirmations overdue by more than five days has tripled. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The metric is a KPI only: it measures back-oﬀice performance, and it cannot serve as a KRI because it records events that have already happened.
The metric is a KCI only, because any metric linked to a control must be classified as a control indicator rather than as a risk indicator.
The metric should leave the KRI set, because KRIs must measure the impact of a risk and overdue confirmations say nothing about loss size.
The metric can act at once as a KPI, a KRI and a KCI: poor back-oﬀice performance, a higher risk of disputes or rogue trading, and a failing control.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – GARP’s own example**

“The failure of a control function is jointly a KPI, a KRI, and a KCI. For example, overdue confirmations of financial transactions can indicate poor back-oﬀice performance (KPI); increased risk of legal disputes, processing errors, or rogue trading (KRI); and signal control failures in transaction processing (KCI).”

⇒ D restates the example.

**Step 2 – The general rule**

“A key control failure always constitutes a source of risk”, and “a KPI turning amber becomes a KRI”.

**Interpretation**

The categories describe the angle from which a metric is read, not boxes that exclude each other (Figure 1).

**LO:** ORR-4 c: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs). • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.4, 4.2 Key Indicators: Performance, Risks and Controls

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.4 (4.2) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-4 c.4)

a.reason: Absolute claim. Rising overdue confirmations signal a rising likelihood of future losses, which is what a preventive KRI does.

b.reason: Absolute claim. GARP’s point is that control indicators and risk indicators overlap.

c.reason: Scope error. KRIs measure likelihood or impact; this one is a likelihood KRI.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
questions.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
questions.topic: Risk Mitigation
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.5 (5.2 Control Automation)
questions.question: The chief operating oﬀicer of a payments bank plans to replace a manual four-eyes check on outgoing payments with an automated, rule-based validation control. Which of the following statements best describes the effect on the bank’s risk profile?

options.text: Automation removes the risk of control failure, because a coded rule is executed in exactly the same way every time.
Automation lowers both the likelihood and the impact of control failures, so the payment control no longer needs to be tested.
Automation converts technology and model risk into human error risk, which is easier for line managers to supervise.
Automation turns frequent, small manual errors into a rarer but potentially large systemic breakdown, and adds technology and model risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What automation gains**

Reliability: the rule runs every time, which removes most isolated human errors.

**Step 2 – What it costs**

“The shift from manual control to automated control transforms the high-likelihood/low-impact risks of isolated manual errors into the low-likelihood/high-impact risk of a systemic control breakdown”, and adds the risk that the system fails or the code is wrong or outdated.

⇒ D (Figure 1).

**Interpretation**

The water mattress: effective mitigation trades the risks we do not want for risks we can accept, and then controls those. Here that means testing the rule, escalating alerts, and planning for downtime.

**LO:** ORR-5 c: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.5, 5.2 Control Automation

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.5 (5.2 Control Automation) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-5 c.2)

a.reason: Absolute claim: the system can fail or the code can be wrong; the risk changes form, it does not disappear.

b.reason: Polarity flip on impact, and automated controls still need testing (examination suits them).

c.reason: Direction reversed: human-error risk becomes technology and model risk.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
questions.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
questions.topic: Risk Mitigation
questions.question: Knight Capital, then the largest market maker in the world, lost nearly USD 460 million in about 45 minutes after new routing code generated millions of erroneous orders. Which of the following best describes the ultimate cause identified in the reading?

options.text: A rogue trader who concealed positions in suspense accounts, made possible by weak segregation of duties between front and back oﬀice.
Code repurposing, weak version control, insuﬀicient testing, unprioritized alerts, and no one with authority to activate the circuit breaker.
A cyberattack that exploited an unpatched vulnerability in the routing system, with an expired certificate that blinded network monitoring.
Excessive reliance on manual controls in order routing, which could not keep pace with the speed of algorithmic trading.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The facts**

Poorly tested new code in the routing system turned 212 small retail orders into millions of erroneous orders in 154 stocks: 397 million shares, a gross exposure of nearly USD 7 billion, a loss of nearly USD 460 million in 45 minutes, and an emergency capital infusion of about USD 400 million.

**Step 2 – GARP’s diagnosis**

“A perfect storm of code repurposing, inadequate version control, insuﬀicient testing, lack of prioritization of alerts, and the absence of an incident response procedure and someone with the authority to activate the circuit breaker.”

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Knight is the reading’s case for automation risk: an automated process failing at machine speed, where early detection and escalation of alerts would have mattered most.

**LO:** ORR-5 c: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.5, Box 5.1 Case Study: The Massive Knight Capital Trading Loss

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.5 (Box 5.1) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-5 c.3)

a.reason: Case cross-mapping: concealed positions and missing segregation of duties describe rogue trading cases, not Knight.

c.reason: Case cross-mapping: an unpatched vulnerability and an expired certificate are the Equifax lessons (ORR-9).

d.reason: Polarity flip: the failure was in automated systems and their controls, not in manual controls.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
questions.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
questions.topic: Risk Mitigation
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.5 (5.2 Control Testing)
questions.question: An operational risk manager is reviewing a bank’s annual control testing plan. Which of the following plans is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Test the key manual control over high-value wire transfers through self-certification by its owner, who knows the control best.
Have the central operational risk function perform all control tests itself, because it owns the firm’s operational risk framework.
Test the key wire-transfer control by observation or reperformance, by a tester independent of its owner and more often than low-risk controls.
Test every control once a year on the same small sample, so that the results are comparable across all controls of the bank.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Match test to control**

A key control over a high-risk activity calls for strong testing: observation (“suitable for key controls”) or reperformance, the strongest form.

**Step 2 – Apply the effectiveness factors**

The tester should be independent of the control owner; frequency should be proportionate to the severity of the risk, with more frequent assessment for higher risks.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The ladder in Section 3 maps risk to scrutiny: self-certification for secondary or low-risk controls, examination for automated controls, observation for key controls, reperformance where the stakes are highest.

**LO:** ORR-5 c: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.5, 5.2 Control Effectiveness; Control Testing and Risk Governance

ORR-7 • Integrated Risk Management • Vardeez: UNTIERED (crash-course notes)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.5 (5.2 Control Testing) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-5 c.6)

a.reason: Self-certification provides no evidence and should be limited to secondary controls or low inherent risk.

b.reason: The ORM function does not usually test controls; it needs assurance from internal audit and the first line.

d.reason: Frequency should follow risk severity, and samples must be representative; small identical samples can give a false view of effectiveness.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.
questions.reading: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
questions.topic: Integrated Risk Management
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Canadian bank is reviewing a board paper that compares the bank’s regulatory capital with its economic capital. Which of the following statements is correct for the paper to include?

options.text: Regulatory capital is a formula-driven minimum set by industrywide rules and is not very risk sensitive; economic capital is the bank’s own estimate for unexpected losses.
Economic capital is set by the supervisor under Pillar 1, while regulatory capital is the bank’s own internal estimate of its unexpected losses under Pillar 2.
Because regulatory capital is calibrated to the bank’s own risk profile, the regulatory and economic figures must be equal for every business line.
Economic capital always exceeds regulatory capital, because it adds the bank’s own buffer on top of the regulatory minimum for each business line.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Regulatory capital**

The Basel minimum: 8% of RWA plus buffers under Pillar 1, adjusted under Pillar 2. GARP: it “is not very risk sensitive and is unlikely to fully reflect the risk profile of the firm”; Crouhy (ORR-18) calls it “a set of industrywide rules and formulas” that “sets only a minimum”.

**Step 2 – Economic capital**

The own funds the firm “judges necessary to cover for any unexpected loss”, from internal models plus overlays, sized to its target rating.

⇒ A states the D3 discrimination.

**Interpretation**

The two answer different questions: the regulator’s “what is the least this bank must hold?” and the bank’s “what do we need to survive at our chosen confidence level?”.

**LO:** ORR-7 b: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.7, 7.3 The Role of Regulatory Capital; The Role of Economic Capital; Ch.18, 18.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.3) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-7 b.1)

b.reason: Sibling swap: the regulator sets regulatory capital; the bank estimates economic capital.

c.reason: Regulatory capital is not calibrated to the firm’s profile, and the two can differ widely by business line.

d.reason: Absolute claim: GARP never says economic capital always exceeds the regulatory figure; for some activities regulatory capital is the higher one (see the correction box).

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.
questions.reading: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
questions.topic: Integrated Risk Management
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.3 The Role of Regulatory Capital)
questions.question: A risk analyst is summarizing the evolution of Basel regulatory capital for new graduates. Which of the following statements is accurate?

options.text: Basel I (1988) set capital for credit, market and operational risk at 8% of RWA, and Basel II raised that ratio when it introduced the three pillars.
Pillar 2 is market discipline through mandatory disclosures, and Pillar 3 is the supervisory review that adds capital for risks not captured by Pillar 1.
Basel III left the overall requirement at 8% of RWA, adding only a minimum liquidity ratio and no further capital requirement for banks.
The 8% of RWA set for credit risk in 1988 stayed unchanged when market risk was added in 1996 and operational risk in Basel II, which introduced three pillars.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The timeline**

1988 Basel I: 8% of RWA for credit risk only. 1996: extended to market risk with VaR, “although the overall minimum requirement of 8% RWA did not change”. 2002 Basel II: operational risk added, credit capital reformed, the three pillars introduced; “the overall requirement of 8% of RWA … remained unchanged”.

⇒ D.

**Step 2 – Basel III**

A minimum liquidity ratio and an additional 2.5% of RWA on top of the 8%.

**Interpretation**

The 8% is the constant of the story; what changed was the scope of risks covered and, with Basel II, the move beyond capital to supervision and disclosure.

**LO:** ORR-7 b: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.7, 7.3 The Role of Regulatory Capital

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.3 The Role of Regulatory Capital) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-7 b.3)

a.reason: Basel I covered credit risk only, and the 8% was not raised by Basel II.

b.reason: Pillars swapped: Pillar 2 is supervisory review, Pillar 3 market discipline.

c.reason: Basel III added 2.5% of RWA on top of the 8% minimum (the capital conservation buffer).

questions.loText: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.
questions.reading: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
questions.topic: Integrated Risk Management
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.3 The Role of Economic Capital)
questions.question: The CFO of a bank that targets an AA rating asks how the target drives the bank’s economic capital. On average, AAA-rated firms have a one-year default probability of 1 basis point and AA-rated firms of 3 basis points. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The bank should size economic capital to cover unexpected losses at 99.97%; an AAA target would mean 99.99% and more capital.
The bank should size economic capital at 99.9%, the regulatory confidence level, because economic capital must use the Pillar 1 standard.
A higher target rating allows a lower confidence level, because a better-rated bank is less likely to default and needs less capital.
Economic capital is unrelated to the credit rating, which depends only on the bank’s regulatory capital ratio under Pillar 1.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the rating as a default probability**

A 3 basis point default probability for AA means losses may exceed capital with probability 0.03%: GARP, “a bank aiming for an AA rating will calculate its economic capital such that it covers unexpected losses for any risk at a 99.97% confidence interval”.

**Step 2 – Move the target**

AAA (1 basis point) means 99.99%, further into the tail, so more capital (Figure 1).

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

Capital buys creditworthiness: “the larger the capital, the bigger the buffer against losses, the better the creditworthiness, the lower the costs of raising funds.”

**LO:** ORR-7 b: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.7, 7.3 The Role of Economic Capital, Figure 7.4

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.3 The Role of Economic Capital) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-7 b.4)

b.reason: Economic capital is the firm’s own choice, set by its target rating, not by the 99.9% regulatory standard.

c.reason: Polarity flip: a higher rating needs a higher confidence level and more capital.

d.reason: GARP links the level of economic capital directly to the maintenance of the credit rating.

questions.loText: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.
questions.reading: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
questions.topic: Integrated Risk Management
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.3 RAROC)
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the use of economic capital in RAROC, as presented in the integrated risk management reading, is correct?

options.text: RAROC divides expected after-tax risk-adjusted net income by regulatory capital, which makes the measure comparable across banks.
RAROC is used mainly for operational risk, because operational losses can be attributed directly to the revenues that generate them.
RAROC is most straightforward for credit activities, where expected loss can be estimated from history, and is generally not used for operational risk.
For market risk, expected loss is usually large and easy to estimate, so RAROC is easier to apply to trading activities than to lending.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The formula**

RAROC = expected after-tax risk-adjusted net income / economic capital: the numerator adjusts income for EL, the denominator is the equity needed for the risks taken.

**Step 2 – Where it works**

“RAROC is more straightforward for credit activities, where EL can be estimated using historical data, than for market risk, where EL is less straightforward and is often set at 0. RAROC is generally not used for operational risk.”

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

Operational risk is hard to attribute to revenues and its economic capital is uncertain, so it is managed through appetite, controls and resilience more than through RAROC.

**LO:** ORR-7 b: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations. • **Reference:** GARP, Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch.7, 7.3 RAROC: Risk-Adjusted Return on Capital

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.3 RAROC) (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-7 b.5)

a.reason: The denominator is economic capital, not regulatory capital.

b.reason: Reversed: RAROC is generally not used for operational risk.

d.reason: For market risk, EL is less straightforward and often set at 0.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe practices for the governance of risks of interconnected third-party service providers.
questions.reading: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
questions.topic: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.8, Section 8.6 and Box 8.8
questions.question: The head of internal audit at a Dutch bank must give the audit committee assurance over a cloud service provider that hosts two of the bank’s critical functions. Seven other European banks use the same provider. Which of the following approaches is consistent with the supervisory practices observed by the Basel Committee?

options.text: Rely on the provider being a licensed specialist provider, since a licence moves ultimate responsibility for the outsourced functions to the provider.
Base the audit opinion on a pooled audit organised with the other banks, or on the provider’s external auditor’s report, where the jurisdiction accepts it.
Keep the right to inspect and audit with the bank alone, since no jurisdiction grants such rights directly to supervisors.
Treat the provider’s compliance testing as settled, since most regulations are aligned on how compliance should be verified.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The audit right**

Most requirements make supervised organisations guarantee “rights to inspect and audit” their providers; some cascade the right to significant subcontractors, and France, Switzerland and Singapore grant it directly to supervisors.

**Step 2 – The basis for the opinion**

“For several jurisdictions the audit opinion on the outsourcing arrangements may be formed based on the report of the service provider’s external auditor. Others accept pooled audits, organised by multiple financial institutions”, or the provider’s internal audit under conditions. In June 2018 eight European institutions jointly audited a common cloud provider.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Pooled and shared audit reporting on critical interconnections can make audits more effective and eﬀicient. It does not change who is accountable: the bank still forms and owns the opinion.

**LO:** ORR-8 e: Describe practices for the governance of risks of interconnected third-party service providers. • **Refer-**

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.8, Section 8.6 and Box 8.8 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-8 e.5)

a.reason: Role misassignment: even for licensed specialist providers (Luxembourg’s PSFs) “the ultimate responsibility remains with the institution”.

c.reason: False fact: France, Switzerland and Singapore grant the right directly to supervisory authorities.

d.reason: False fact: “most regulations are not aligned in terms of how compliance should be verified or tested”.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe practices for the governance of risks of interconnected third-party service providers.
questions.reading: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
questions.topic: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.8, Section 8.6 and footnote 20
questions.question: A mid-sized European bank runs core banking, card payments, customer-data storage and its disaster-recovery site on one cloud service provider, which sub-outsources data-centre operations. The head of third-party risk is drafting a paper for the board on the bank’s concentration risk and its resilience implications. Based on the Basel Committee’s range of practices, which of the following statements should the paper include?

options.text: Concentration risk here means the systemic risk to the banking industry from many banks using one provider, so it is for supervisors to address rather than for the bank.
Continuity testing can stay confined to the bank’s own systems, because observed supervisory expectations focus on each institution’s standalone business continuity.

Concentration risk here means the bank’s possible lack of control over one provider running several of its activities; the bank should set end-to-end recovery objectives and plan a prompt transfer to another provider.
Keeping the disaster-recovery site with the same provider is preferable, because adding a second provider would raise the bank’s vendor lock-in risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Define concentration risk in this report**

“Concentration risk” here “does not refer to the potential systemic risk to the industry as a whole, but rather to the potential lack of control of an individual firm over one single provider as multiple activities are outsourced to the same service provider”.

⇒ A firm-level risk the bank must manage.

**Step 2 – The resilience response**

Recovery and resumption objectives are set “for critical business activities from an end-to-end perspective”; plans include “planned redundancy, so as to ensure the prompt transfer of outsourced activities to a different provider”; critical suppliers’ continuity plans are aligned with the bank’s; tests use realistic scenarios at least yearly.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

Four activities, including the recovery site, on one provider (and its subcontractor) is a single point of failure. The paper should map the dependency end to end, align and test the provider’s plans with the bank’s, and keep a real exit route.

**LO:** ORR-8 e: Describe practices for the governance of risks of interconnected third-party service providers. • **Ref-** **erence:** BCBS (2018), GARP ORR Ch.8, Section 8.6 (Governance of Third-Party Connections, footnote 20; Business Continuity and Availability)

ORR-17 • Stress Testing Banks • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.8, Section 8.6 and footnote 20 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-8 e.6)

a.reason: Scope error: footnote 20 explicitly excludes industry-wide systemic risk from the meaning used here.

b.reason: True fact, wrong conclusion: observed expectations do centre on standalone continuity, but where critical activities depend on third parties regulators stress aligned plans and testing, and the report sees room to extend testing across the ecosystem.

d.reason: Polarity flip: vendor lock-in is the inability to withdraw and transfer the activity; a second provider reduces it, while a recovery site at the same provider fails with the production systems.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
questions.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
questions.topic: Stress Testing Banks
questions.question: An internal auditor at a European bank is reviewing a training module on the supervisory stress tests run in the US and Europe between 2009 and 2012. Which of the following statements in the module is correct?

options.text: Post-SCAP stress testing replaced single-factor shocks with a broad macro scenario applied firm-wide, but like pre-SCAP testing it remained static and confined to projected losses.
The 2011 CCAR asked banks to submit results under their own baseline and stress scenarios in addition to the common supervisory scenario, but published no bank-level results.
The 2011 EBA stress test applied Basel I risk weights, so banks needed only stressed default rates rather than full stressed rating migration matrices to project RWA.
All four Irish banks failed the 2010 CEBS stress test, which led directly to the March 2011 Irish exercise that revealed a capital need of EUR 24 billion.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Pre- versus post-SCAP (Table 17.2)**

Post-SCAP testing is a broad macro scenario with market stress, comprehensive and firm-wide, dynamic and path dependent, tied to an explicit post-stress common equity threshold, and covers losses, revenues and costs.

**Step 2 – Regime facts (Tables 17.1 and 17.3, Sections 17.3 and 17.5)**

CCAR, in operation since 2011, “asks banks to submit results using their own scenarios (baseline and stress) in addition to results under the common supervisory stress scenario”. The 2011 CCAR disclosure: “only the macro-scenario was published, with no bank-level results”; banks allowed to raise dividends were read as having passed.

⇒ The dual approach lets supervisors compare banks on the common scenario while learning what each bank thinks its own high-risk scenarios are.

**Interpretation**

B is correct. Contrast the 2009 SCAP (bank-level stress losses by asset class, supervisory estimates, stress results only) and the 2012 CCAR (near-SCAP detail; four of 19 did not pass in the sense of receiving an objection to their capital plans).

**LO:** ORR-17 a: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests. • **Reference:** Schuermann, Stress Testing Banks, International Journal of Forecasting 30:3 (2014), Sections 17.1, 17.3, 17.5; Tables 17.1, 17.2, 17.3

ORR-17 • Stress Testing Banks • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook C5.2 • S1, S5 • Map #30 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-17 a.8)

a.reason: Scope/condition error: the first clause is true, but post-SCAP testing is dynamic and path dependent and covers revenues and costs as well as losses; “static, losses only” describes pre-SCAP testing.

c.reason: Sibling swap: Basel I weights belong to the US exercises (SCAP, CCAR). The EBA test used Basel II weights, which are ratings sensitive, so banks had to use stress migration matrices to project the whole future ratings distribution, not just defaults.

d.reason: Polarity flip (case cross-mapping): “all of these banks had previously passed the CEBS stress test”. The EUR 24 billion need for the four banks came from the 2011 exercise run largely by outside advisors after Ireland requested EU and IMF assistance.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.
questions.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
questions.topic: Stress Testing Banks
questions.question:
A supervisory policy analyst compares the design of two macro-prudential stress tests discussed by Schuermann:

| Test | Scenario length | Post-stress hurdle |
|---|---|---|
| 2009 SCAP (United States) | Two years | 4% Tier 1 common |
| 2012 bottom-up test (Spain) | Three years | 6% core Tier 1 |

Which of the following conclusions about the design of these tests is most appropriate?

options.text: The Spanish authorities showed a higher risk appetite, because a longer scenario spreads the same losses over more years and makes the test easier to pass.
The Spanish authorities showed a lower risk appetite, because their banks had to remain better capitalized after a longer period of stress.
SCAP was the more severe test, because its lower post-stress hurdle implies that its scenario assumed larger losses.
The two tests can be ranked on overall severity by the “1 in 100” probability statements that supervisors attach to their multivariate scenarios.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the two numbers measure**

The authorities’ risk appetite fixes “how severe and how long the stress scenario should be, and what the post-stress hurdle is”. In the sailing analogy: how long is the storm, and how solid must the boat be once it has passed.

**Step 2 – Compare**

Spain asked for a longer storm (three years against two) and a more solid boat afterwards (6% against 4%). Both make the test more demanding.

⇒ GARP: the Spanish design suggests “a lower risk appetite by the Spanish authorities than by the American”.

**Interpretation**

Length and hurdle are the easy dimensions to compare. Scenario severity is the hard one, which is why option D fails.

**LO:** ORR-17 b: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors. • **Reference:** Schuermann, GARP ORR Ch.17, Section 17.3

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-17 b.2)

a.reason: Polarity flip: a longer horizon accumulates more stress losses before the hurdle is tested; it does not dilute them.

c.reason: Confuses the hurdle with severity: the hurdle is the capital the bank must keep after the stress, not a measure of how severe the scenario is.

d.reason: Absolute claim: authorities are reluctant to make “1 in 100” statements because they are hard to make credibly; the Fed publishes variable time series so users can judge severity variable by variable.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.
questions.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
questions.topic: Stress Testing Banks
questions.question: The head of enterprise stress testing at a European bank is auditing the bank’s scenario-design manual against the lessons Schuermann draws from the supervisory stress tests. Which of the following provisions should the head retain?

options.text: Each scenario shocks one risk factor at a time to an extreme value, holding the others at current levels, so that the source of every loss is easy to attribute.
Because a historical scenario is coherent by construction, the bank replays only the market moves of June to December 2008, which also ensures that new vulnerabilities are tested.
The bank runs only the common supervisory scenario, since adding a bank-specific scenario would prevent supervisors from comparing results across banks.
A flight-to-quality scenario that also stresses the bank’s holdings of highly rated sovereign bonds must name the alternative asset class to which capital flees.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What a flight to quality requires**

A scenario with a flight from risky assets must contain a (usually small) set of safe-haven assets, typically the bonds of the safest sovereigns. Questioning the safety of those sovereigns is a worthwhile scenario, “but it would need to define an alternative ‘risk-free’ asset class to which capital can flee”.

⇒ D keeps the scenario coherent and should be retained.

**Step 2 – Audit the other provisions**

A is the single-shock design SCAP left behind. B relies on history alone. C ignores CCAR’s dual approach.

**Interpretation**

This is the C9·S1 audit shape: what to stress (joint, offsetting moves), what to avoid (single factors, history alone, one size for all).

**LO:** ORR-17 b: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors. • **Reference:** Schuermann, GARP ORR Ch.17, Section 17.3

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-17 b.5)

a.reason: One factor at a time is incoherent: when one factor moves significantly, the others move too.

b.reason: Half true: a historical scenario gives loose coherence, but “it does not test for anything new”.

c.reason: False trade-off: CCAR keeps the common scenario for comparison and adds banks’ own scenarios to reveal their specific vulnerabilities, “without sacrificing risk-discovery”.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
questions.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
questions.topic: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
questions.question: An internal auditor at a large US bank holding company subject to the Capital Plan Rule is assessing the BHC’s capital planning process against the Federal Reserve’s description of the range of current practice. Which of the following observations should the auditor record as consistent with stronger practice?

options.text: The BHC’s own stress scenario produces lower post-stress capital ratios than the supervisory severely adverse scenario, so its severity is accepted without further support.
Senior management, rather than the board, approves the capital plan, while the board is updated on capital adequacy and post-stress capital measures at least quarterly.
Where management overlays adjust modeled loss estimates, the board receives both the unadjusted model results and the results after the judgmental adjustments.
Wholesale losses under stress are projected with long-run average PD, LGD, and EAD by rating grade, since these averages span both expansions and downturns.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Overlays and reporting (Section 20.7)**

If a BHC makes extensive adjustments to modeled estimates, “the impact of such adjustments should be quantified relative to unadjusted estimates” and documented for management and the board; “management should always provide both the initial results and the results after any judgmental adjustments”.

⇒ The board can only challenge the result if it sees how far judgment moved the model; extensive overlays should also prompt a review of whether better models are needed.

**Step 2 – Check the other observations against governance and scenario design**

Board approval of the capital plan is required by the Rule (Section 20.4). Scenario severity must come from the BHC’s unique vulnerabilities, and a harsher-than-supervisory outcome is not a safe harbor (Section 20.6). Long-run averages are excluded for stress projection (Section 20.7).

**Interpretation**

C is correct: it is a governance practice (S1) that keeps the board informed of model limitations before capital decisions are made.

**LO:** ORR-20 a: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule. ORR-20 b: Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas: - Risk identification - Internal controls, including model review and validation - Corporate governance - Capital policy, including setting of goals and targets and contingency planning - Stress testing and stress scenario design - Estimating losses, revenues, and expenses, including quantitative and qualitative methodologies - Assessing the impact of capital adequacy, including risk-weighted asset (RWA) and balance sheet projections • **Reference:** Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies (August 2013), Sections 20.4, 20.6, 20.7

ORR-20 • Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D10.1 • S1, S2 • Map #53 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-20 a.7)

a.reason: Absolute claim: “a BHC stress scenario that produces post-stress capital ratios lower than those under the supervisory severely adverse scenario is not, in and of itself, a safe harbor”; the scenario must still target the BHC’s own vulnerabilities and be supported by a clear narrative.

b.reason: Role misassignment: “the board of directors is required to approve a BHC’s capital plan under the Capital Plan Rule”; senior management implements board-authorized activities and makes recommendations to the board. The quarterly information clause is correct.

d.reason: Scope/condition error: “estimates based on long-run average behavior over a mix of conditions, including periods of economic expansion and downturn, are not appropriate for projecting losses under stress and should not be used for these purposes”.

questions.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
questions.topic: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
questions.question: The corporate secretary of a US bank holding company subject to the Capital Plan Rule is drafting a responsibilities matrix for the capital planning process. Which of the following assignments is consistent with the Federal Reserve’s supervisory expectations?

options.text: Senior management approves the final capital distributions in the plan, and the board reviews a summary of capital adequacy once a year after the plan has been submitted.
The board ensures that the stress scenarios are suﬀiciently severe and develops remediation plans for weaknesses in the process, which senior management then reviews.

The board approves the capital plan, the board or a designated board committee approves the capital policy, and the board receives capital information, including post-stress pro forma measures framed against the capital goals and targets, at least quarterly.
The board treats the post-stress capital ratios from enterprise-wide scenario analysis as precise point estimates, so that its decisions do not depend on management’s discussion of model limitations.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the board must do**

“The board of directors is required to approve a BHC’s capital plan under the Capital Plan Rule.” The capital policy “must be approved by the BHC’s board of directors or a designated committee of the board”. The board “should receive this information at least quarterly”, including capital measures “on a post-stress, pro forma basis” framed against the goals and targets.

⇒ C assigns each task correctly.

**Step 2 – What senior management must do**

Ensure effective controls and that “the BHC’s stress scenarios are suﬀiciently severe”; make recommendations on capital goals and distributions; identify weaknesses and develop remediation plans, and report both to the board.

**Interpretation**

This is shape D10·S1 in its purest form: the board approves and challenges; senior management implements, recommends and reports.

**LO:** ORR-20 b: Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas: - Risk identification - Internal controls, including model review and validation - Corporate governance - Capital policy, including setting of goals and targets and contingency planning - Stress testing and stress scenario design - Estimating losses, revenues, and expenses, including quantitative and qualitative methodologies - Assessing the impact of capital adequacy, including risk-weighted asset (RWA) and balance sheet projections • **Reference:** Federal Reserve, GARP ORR Ch.20, Sections 20.4 and 20.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-20 b.4)

a.reason: Role misassignment and wrong frequency: capital decisions, including distributions, are approved by the board, which receives capital information at least quarterly.

b.reason: Role swap: ensuring severity and developing remediation plans are senior management’s duties, reported to the board.

d.reason: Stronger boards “recognized that internal capital planning results are estimates and should be viewed as part of a range of possible results”; the board needs the limitations to challenge results.

questions.loText: Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas: - Risk identification - Internal controls, including model review and validation - Corporate governance - Capital policy, including setting of goals and targets and contingency planning - Stress testing and stress scenario design - Estimating losses, revenues, and expenses, including quantitative and qualitative methodologies - Assessing the impact of capital adequacy, including risk-weighted asset (RWA) and balance sheet projections

questions.question: A model risk oﬀicer at a US bank holding company is reviewing the balance sheet and RWA projections that feed the post-stress capital ratios under the BHC’s own stress scenario. Which of the following practices is consistent with the Federal Reserve’s expectations?

options.text: Assuming that deposits flow in from weaker competitors in a flight to quality, which lowers the BHC’s dollar cost of funding over the stress horizon.
Reducing projected RWA from the second year onward to reflect enhancements to internal risk models that are scheduled for approval during the horizon.
Accepting a projection in which PPNR rises while loan and deposit balances decline, because wider margins in stress offset the lower volumes.
Projecting loan balances from their drivers (contractual paydowns, modeled prepayments, nonperformance and new business), each checked for consistency with the scenario.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – How balances should be projected**

“BHCs with stronger practices separately considered the drivers of change to asset and funding balances, such as contractual paydowns, modeled prepayments, nonperformance, and new business activity for assets, rather than simply projecting targeted balances directly.”

⇒ D is the stronger practice.

**Step 2 – The favorable assumptions**

GARP lists as aggressive: large asset-mix changes that cut risk weights, “flight-to-quality” assumptions and funding mix changes that increase deposits and reduce the cost of funding (A), significant shrinkage without its losses, and operating margin improvement. Separately, BHCs “should not assume any RWA reductions from potential data or model enhancements” (B), and “an increase in PPNR amid declining balances would appear generally inconsistent” (C).

**Interpretation**

The aggregation step is where these inconsistencies surface; a central group should challenge them rather than accept them.

**LO:** ORR-20 b: Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas: - Risk identification - Internal controls, including model review and validation - Corporate governance - Capital policy, including setting of goals and targets and contingency planning - Stress testing and stress scenario design - Estimating losses, revenues, and expenses, including quantitative and qualitative methodologies - Assessing the impact of capital adequacy, including risk-weighted asset (RWA) and balance sheet projections • **Reference:** Federal Reserve, GARP ORR Ch.20, Section 20.8 (Balance Sheet and RWAs; Aggregation of Projections)

ORR-21 • Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis • Vardeez: UNTIERED

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-20 b.10)

a.reason: A flight-to-quality deposit inflow is one of GARP’s four examples of a favorable balance sheet assumption.

b.reason: Planned model enhancements cannot reduce projected RWA.

c.reason: Rising PPNR amid falling balances warrants investigation; assumed margin improvement is itself a favorable assumption.

questions.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
questions.topic: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
questions.question: A trainee at a central bank asks why bank regulation moved from private arrangements to oﬀicial supervision and international coordination. Which of the following explanations is correct?

options.text: Private support arrangements, such as clearinghouses that monitored members’ solvency, could not cope with panics large enough that only an entity able to print money could support the system, so government-controlled central banks became lenders of last resort.
The Basel Committee was created in 1988 to publish Basel I, after the failure of Herstatt Bank showed that banks in countries with low capital minimums held too little equity.
The failure of Herstatt Bank in 1974 was a market risk event, a large trading loss on equities, which is why the first Basel accord set capital for market risk.
Oﬀicial regulation began because private arrangements had no information on members’ finances: clearinghouse members neither shared financial statements nor had rights of inspection.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The limit of private arrangements**

Banks banded together to support each other in runs, and clearinghouses monitored members’ solvency. GARP: “If a panic was big enough, no entity without the power to print money would have enough resources to support the financial system.”

⇒ Government-controlled central banks therefore became lenders of last resort: statement A.

**Step 2 – Where Herstatt and the BCBS fit**

Herstatt failed in 1974; differences in currency delivery times across time zones left large FX transactions unsettled. The BCBS was created the same year in response. Basel I came 14 years later.

**Interpretation**

Two separate causal chains are tested here: private to oﬀicial regulation (panic size, economic cost, customer complaints, globalization), and Herstatt to the BCBS (settlement risk across borders). Basel I’s own motivations are the next question.

**LO:** ORR-21 a: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.21, introduction

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-21 a.1)

b.reason: Wrong date and wrong cause: the BCBS dates from 1974, and Herstatt exposed settlement arrangements, not low capital minimums.

c.reason: Herstatt was a clearing and settlement failure, and Basel I covered credit risk only; market risk capital came with the 1996 Amendment.

d.reason: Polarity flip: clearinghouse members did share financial statements and had rights of inspection. The limit was resources, and the monitoring was private.

questions.loText: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.
questions.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
questions.topic: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
questions.question: A regulatory policy analyst is preparing a slide that pairs each pre-crisis revision of the Basel framework with the problem that prompted it. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: 1995 Amendment, netting: by 1995 the BCBS was confident that master agreements would hold up in bankruptcy, whereas the 1988 rules had penalised hedging by charging an add-on on each offsetting contract.
1996 Amendment, market risk capital: banking crises in the Nordic countries had shown that systemic problems could occur even in well-capitalized banking systems.
Basel II, operational risk capital: the 1987 stock market crash had shown that trading book losses were not captured by credit risk-weighted assets.
Basel II, Pillars 2 and 3: supervisors wanted to remove national discretion entirely by replacing field supervisors’ judgement with uniform rules.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The 1995 Amendment**

The original Basel I gave almost no capital credit for netting: each of two offsetting swaps drew an add-on, which disincentivized hedging, because in 1988 master agreements “had not been suﬀiciently tested in bankruptcy courts”. By 1995 the BCBS was more confident.

⇒ Statement A pairs the change with its stated reason.

**Step 2 – Re-pair the distractors**

1996 Amendment: the 1987 crash, VaR in widespread use, trading book market risk not captured. Basel II: Basel I not risk-based enough, the Nordic crises, technical advances, and Barings for operational risk. The pillars were a push toward convergence of national practice.

**Interpretation**

The S4 shape lists real reasons attached to the wrong revision. Anchor each revision to its trigger: hedging penalty (1995), trading losses and VaR (1996), risk insensitivity and Nordic crises (Basel II).

**LO:** ORR-21 a: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.21, 21.1 (Netting; The 1995 and 1996 Amendments) and 21.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-21 a.5)

b.reason: The Nordic banking crises are one of GARP’s reasons for Basel II, not for the 1996 market risk amendment.

c.reason: The 1987 crash is a reason for the 1996 market risk charge. Operational risk capital followed losses such as Barings.

d.reason: Absolute claim. Pillars 2 and 3 pushed national practices toward convergence: national discretion “was reduced”, not removed, and Pillar 2 relies on supervisors’ judgement of each bank’s ICAAP.

questions.topic: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
questions.source: Workbook C5.1 • S2, S3, S4 • Map #30
questions.question: A regulatory policy analyst at a Canadian bank is presenting a timeline of the Basel accords, from Basel I to the December 2017 reforms, to a group of newly hired analysts. Which of the following statements is correct for the analyst to include?

options.text: Basel I required Tier 1 capital of at least 4% and total capital of at least 8% of risk-weighted assets, with Tier 2 capital allowed to make up as much as two-thirds of total capital.
The December 2017 reforms replaced the Basel II output floor, set at 80% of Basel I capital requirements, with a floor on standardised-approach RWA phased in from 50% in 2022 to 72.5% in 2027.

Basel II required internationally active banks to use the standardised approach for credit risk and reserved the IRB approaches for banks whose internal risk measures could not support more granular weights.
The December 2017 reforms widened the use of internal models by introducing an internally modelled approach for CVA risk and by retaining the AMA for banks with ten years of loss data.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Place each claim in its accord**

Basel I (1988): risk-based ratios and capital definitions. Basel II (2004): credit risk options and the three pillars. December 2017 Basel III reforms: revised standardised approaches, constrained internal models, output floor.

**Step 2 – Test the output floor claim against ORR-23 c**

The Basel II floor was “calibrated at 80% of the relevant Basel I capital requirements” and was applied inconsistently. It is replaced by a floor based on the revised Basel III standardised approaches: RWA is the higher of RWA under approved approaches and 72.5% of RWA under the standardised approaches only, with the transitional percentage rising 50%, 55%, 60%, 65%, 70% and 72.5% from 1 January 2022 to 1 January 2027 (Table 23.5).

⇒ The floor limits the capital benefit an internal-models bank can draw relative to a standardised bank, keeping a level playing field and supporting comparability.

**Interpretation**

B is correct. It joins S3 (the two floors) to S4 (Basel II to Basel III progression); the other three statements each corrupt one attribute of the standardised versus internal-models split or of Basel I.

**LO:** ORR-21 a: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time. ORR-23 c: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor. • **Reference:** Carey, Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis (Basel I; Basel II, Capital for Credit Risk); BCBS, High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (Output Floor; Table 23.5; CVA Risk Framework; Operational Risk Framework) ORR-21 • Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis • Vardeez: UNTIERED

**Source:** Workbook C5.1 • S2, S3, S4 • Map #30 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-21 a.6)

a.reason: Scope/condition error: Basel I capped Tier 2 at no more than half of total capital; Tier 1 above 4% could be counted toward the 8% requirement, not the other way round.

c.reason: Role misassignment: the roles are reversed. The standardised approach was “intended for banks with internal risk measures and risk management practices that were insuﬀicient to support the IRB approaches”; the United States did not implement it and required internationally active banks to use IRB.

d.reason: Polarity flip: the reforms removed the internal model for CVA risk (leaving SA-CVA and BA-CVA) and replaced the AMA with a single standardised approach for all banks.

questions.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
questions.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
questions.topic: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
questions.question:
A credit risk oﬀicer at a Belgian bank in 1993 is computing the bank’s minimum total capital under the original Basel I guidelines. The bank’s exposures (EUR million) are:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| On balance sheet |  |
| Cash | 40 |
| Bonds issued by OECD central governments | 160 |
| Claims on OECD banks | 100 |
| Uninsured residential mortgages | 300 |
| Loans to corporations | 500 |
| Off balance sheet |  |
| Transaction-related standby letters of credit; counterparty an OECD bank | 80 |
| Undrawn commitments to corporations, original maturity two years | 200 |
| Undrawn commitments to corporations, original maturity six months | 150 |

Credit conversion factors: transaction-related standby letters of credit 50%; commitments with an original maturity of one year or more 20%; under one year 0%. Which of the following is closest to the bank’s minimum total capital?

options.text: EUR 28.72 million
EUR 53.60 million
EUR 57.44 million
EUR 60.00 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – On-balance-sheet RWA**

0 × 40 + 0 × 160 + 20% × 100 + 50% × 300 + 100% × 500 = 0 + 0 + 20 + 150 + 500 = 670

**Step 2 – Convert the off-balance-sheet items**

Standby letters of credit 50% × 80 = 40; two-year commitments 20% × 200 = 40; six-month commitments 0% × 150 = 0.

**Step 3 – Apply the counterparty weights**

40 × 20% + 40 × 100% = 8 + 40 = 48

⇒ The standby letters of credit take the 20% weight of the OECD bank counterparty.

**Step 4 – RWA and capital**

RWA $= 670 + 48 = 718, 8\% \times718 = \text{EUR} 57.44$ million

**Interpretation**

At least half, EUR 28.72 million (4% × 718), must be Tier 1. The EUR 150 million of six-month commitments add nothing: short commitments convert at 0%.

**LO:** ORR-21 b: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.21, 21.1 (Risk-Weighted Assets; Tables 21.1 and 21.2)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-21 b.5)

a.reason: Applied the 4% Tier 1 floor instead of the 8% total requirement: 4%×718 = 28.72.

b.reason: Left out the off-balance-sheet items: 8% × 670 = 53.60.

d.reason: Converted the standby letters of credit but did not apply the OECD bank’s 20% weight: RWA = 670 + 40 + 40 = 750, 8% × 750 = 60.00.
