questions.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
questions.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
questions.topic: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
questions.question:
The head of regulatory reporting at a Portuguese bank is summarizing for the audit committee what changed in Pillar 1 when the bank moved from Basel I (with the 1996 Amendment) to Basel

II. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The minimum total capital ratio stayed at 8% of risk-weighted assets, but operational risk RWA were added to credit and market risk RWA, while the 1996 treatment of market risk was carried over largely unchanged.
The minimum total capital ratio rose from 8% to 10.5% of risk-weighted assets, because Basel II added a capital conservation buffer on top of the minimum.
Basel II replaced the 1996 internal models approach for market risk with a charge that adds a stressed VaR term to the current VaR term.
Under the Basel II standardized approach, OECD membership remained the basis for sovereign and bank risk weights, with external ratings used only for corporate exposures.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What Pillar 1 kept**

The 8% minimum on RWA and the 1996 market risk charge (standardized method or internal VaR models).

**Step 2 – What Pillar 1 changed**

Operational risk RWA joined the denominator, and credit risk weights became risk-sensitive: ratings under the standardized approach, internal estimates under IRB.

⇒ Statement A.

**Interpretation**

Basel II rebuilt the measurement of risk inside the same 8% ratio. Higher minimums and buffers had to wait for Basel III.

**LO:** ORR-21 d: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.21, 21.2 (Basel II; The Standardized Approach)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-21 d.2)

b.reason: Wrong accord: the 2.5% capital conservation buffer (8% plus 2.5% = 10.5%) is Basel III.

c.reason: Wrong accord: the stressed VaR term is Basel 2.5 (in force by end-2011); Basel II left market risk on the 1996 basis.

d.reason: Polarity flip: OECD status no longer matters under the Basel II standardized approach; ratings set the weights for sovereigns and banks as well as corporates.

questions.loText: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.
questions.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
questions.topic: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
questions.question: The head of a credit trading desk at a German bank is drafting the documentation for the desk’s incremental risk charge model. The desk holds corporate bonds in the trading book. Which of the following statements in the draft is correct?

options.text: Each bond is assigned a liquidity horizon, and for the most liquid bonds the horizon may be set as short as one month.
A bond downgraded from AA to A within its six-month liquidity horizon is assumed sold at the end of the horizon, with the loss recorded, and replaced by an AA-rated bond.
Because the portfolio is rebalanced to its initial credit quality, the constant level of risk assumption generally increases the one-year 99.9% VaR relative to holding the positions all year.
The charge is a 10-day 99% VaR of default losses only, multiplied by a factor of at least three, as for general market risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The replacement rule**

“Any position that is downgraded or that defaults is replaced by a position with the same pre-downgrade rating. A loss is recorded from sale of the downgraded or defaulted position.”

⇒ B describes this exactly: sell at the end of the horizon, book the loss, buy AA again.

**Step 2 – Check the other three against the rules**

The replacement period “differs across positions according to their liquidity but is never less than three months”. Rebalancing keeps credit quality roughly constant and generally reduces the 99.9% VaR. The calibration is one-year 99.9%, covering downgrades as well as defaults.

**Interpretation**

The process is: liquidity horizon per position, simulate defaults and downgrades, rebalance at each horizon, take the 99.9th percentile of the one-year loss.

**LO:** ORR-22 b: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.22, 22.2 Incremental Risk Charge; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 3, Reading 63, LO 63.b

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.22 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-22 b.5)

a.reason: The floor is three months; one month is not allowed.

c.reason: Polarity flip: rebalancing makes default less likely, so it generally lowers the one-year 99.9% VaR.

d.reason: Describes the market risk VaR with its multiplier, restricted to defaults; the IRC is one-year 99.9% and includes migration.

questions.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
questions.topic: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
questions.question: The head of the correlation trading desk at a UK bank asks why Basel 2.5 introduced a separate comprehensive risk (CR) charge for the desk instead of relying on the treatment of credit risk in the IRB framework. Which of the following is the best explanation?

options.text: The IRB framework assumes default correlation is zero, which overstates diversification in every credit portfolio, including ordinary loan books.
The Gordy model behind IRB holds correlation constant across obligors and over time; that suits ordinary debt portfolios, but tranche values move sharply when correlations change.
Correlation-sensitive instruments had been placed in the banking book to exploit its lower capital, so the CR charge moves them into the trading book.
Highly rated tranches had defaulted frequently before the crisis, so the CR charge was calibrated to the observed pre-crisis default rates of AAA tranches.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The IRB assumption**

Basel II assumes the Gordy (2003) correlation parameter is constant across obligors and over time (though not across asset types).

⇒ Reasonable for portfolios of debt instruments in the banking book.

**Step 2 – Why it fails for the correlation book**

Securitizations issue tranches of different seniority; “correlations change over time and such changes can have large effects on the value of tranches”. AAA tranche prices implied near-zero PD before the crisis and fell when market PD estimates rose.

**Interpretation**

The CR charge exists because tranche value is a function of correlation, which the IRB framework treats as a fixed parameter.

**LO:** ORR-22 c: Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.22, 22.2 Correlations and the Comprehensive Risk Measure

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.22 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-22 c.1)

a.reason: The Gordy model uses a positive, constant correlation, not zero; and GARP calls the assumption reasonable for ordinary debt portfolios.

c.reason: Wrong book and wrong charge: the arbitrage ran into the trading book, where capital was lower, and it is the IRC’s story (ORR-22 b).

d.reason: Polarity flip: pre-crisis prices implied a near-zero PD for AAA tranches; losses came with the crisis.

questions.question: A market risk analyst is classifying positions in the bank’s correlation book for the Basel 2.5 standardized comprehensive risk charge. Which of the following positions should be charged on the re-securitization schedule?

options.text: A CDO whose collateral pool consists of mezzanine tranches issued by residential mortgage securitization vehicles.
A residential mortgage-backed security whose collateral pool consists of prime first-lien mortgages.
A synthetic CDO tranche referencing a portfolio of 100 single-name corporate credit default swaps.
A collateralized loan obligation tranche backed by a pool of leveraged corporate loans.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The definition**

A re-securitization is a securitization whose underlying pool consists of “the tranched liabilities of securitization vehicles”.

**Step 2 – Apply it**

A CDO holding mezzanine RMBS tranches has tranches as collateral: a re-securitization. The RMBS (mortgages), the synthetic CDO (single-name CDS) and the CLO (loans) all reference ordinary assets.

**Interpretation**

Tranches of tranches compound the sensitivity to correlation, which is why the re-securitization schedule is roughly twice the securitization schedule in every rated bucket.

**LO:** ORR-22 c: Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.22, 22.2 Correlations and the Comprehensive Risk Measure; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 3, Reading 63, LO 63.c

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.22 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-22 c.3)

b.reason: Mortgages are ordinary assets: a securitization.

c.reason: A synthetic CDO referencing single-name CDS is a securitization of credit exposures, not of tranches.

d.reason: A CLO pools loans: a securitization.

options.text: The percentages in the table are risk weights, so a BBB securitization requires capital of 8% of exposure multiplied by the 8% minimum capital ratio.
Re-securitizations attract lower charges than securitizations with the same rating, because their underlying pools are themselves diversified tranches.
Tranches rated below BB, or unrated, attract a 100% charge, so in effect the bank must finance such positions entirely with capital.
The charge for a tranche depends on its rating, on its seniority within the deal and on the bank’s own estimate of default correlation.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the table correctly**

The percentages are “capital as a fraction of the exposure, not risk weights”. They depend only on the rating, on the securitization or re-securitization schedule.

**Step 2 – The bottom of the rating scale**

Below BB, or unrated: 100% on both schedules. These tranches are the most exposed to pool losses, so “in effect they must be financed entirely with capital”.

⇒ C is correct.

**Interpretation**

Dollar-for-dollar capital is the standardized approach’s way of saying such a tranche behaves like equity in the underlying pool.

**LO:** ORR-22 c: Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.22, 22.2, Table 22.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.22 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-22 c.4)

a.reason: Treats capital percentages as risk weights; the 8% is already the capital.

b.reason: Polarity flip: re-securitizations are charged more (for example 18% against 8% at BBB).

d.reason: The standardized charge depends only on the rating (and the schedule); bank correlation estimates enter only an approved internal model.

questions.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis

questions.question: A bank applies to its supervisor to calculate the comprehensive risk charge for its correlation book with an internal model. Which of the following conditions applies to the model?

options.text: It must capture multiple default and rating-change events, volatility in correlations and spreads, basis risk, hedge dynamics and recovery volatility, and its charge is floored at a fraction of the standardized charge.
Once approved, it replaces the standardized approach entirely, so the bank no longer needs to compute the standardized charge for the correlation book.
It need only reproduce the incremental risk charge calculation: a one-year 99.9% VaR of default and migration losses under a constant level of risk.
Because it captures hedges more precisely, its charge is expected to exceed the standardized charge, which therefore acts as a cap on the model result.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the model must capture**

“Multiple default and rating change events; volatility in correlations and credit spreads; basis risk (e.g., the difference between CDS and underlying index values); the dynamics of hedges; and volatility in recovery rates”, ideally by full-revaluation simulation.

**Step 2 – The floor**

“The model-based charge may not be less than a fraction of the charge under the standardized approach.”

⇒ A states both conditions.

**Interpretation**

A floor (not a cap) on the model, and an unusually demanding list of risks, because the instruments are complex and the model’s main attraction, better recognition of hedges, is also where it can understate risk.

**LO:** ORR-22 c: Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks. • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.22, 22.2 Correlations and the Comprehensive Risk Measure; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 3, Reading 63, LO 63.c

ORR-22 • Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis • Vardeez: UNTIERED

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.22 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-22 c.6)

b.reason: The standardized charge still matters: it sets the floor.

c.reason: The IRC model (default and migration, constant level of risk) is far from enough; correlation, spread and recovery volatility, basis risk and hedge dynamics are required.

d.reason: Direction reversed: the standardized charge sets a floor under the model, not a cap above it.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).
questions.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
questions.topic: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
questions.question:
A capital planning analyst at a European G-SIB in the 1.5% bucket is computing the bank’s fully buffered CET1 requirement. RWA are EUR 400 billion. The bank’s private-sector credit exposures and the countercyclical buffer rates that apply to them are:

| Country | Share of exposures | CCyB rate |
|---|---|---|
| Home country X | 50% | 1.0% |
| Country Y | 30% | 2.5% |
| Country Z | 20% | 0.0% |

Which of the following is closest to the minimum CET1 capital the bank must hold in normal times, including all buffers?

options.text: EUR 33.0 billion
EUR 38.0 billion
EUR 39.0 billion
EUR 44.0 billion

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Weighted CCyB**

0.50(1.0%) + 0.30(2.5%) + 0.20(0%) = 0.50% + 0.75% = 1.25%

⇒ An international bank’s CCyB is a weighted average of the national rates.

**Step 2 – Fully buffered CET1 ratio**

$$4.5\% + 2.5\% (\text{CCB}) + 1.5\% (\text{G-SIB}) + 1.25\% (\text{CCyB}) = 9.75\%$$

**Step 3 – Amount**

$9.75\% \times400 = \text{EUR} 39.0$ billion

**Interpretation**

The CCyB follows the location of the bank’s exposures, not its headquarters. A simple average of the three rates (1.17%) would give EUR 38.7 billion, close to the answer but wrong in principle.

**LO:** ORR-22 e: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs). • **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.22, 22.3 Buffers

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.22 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-22 e.7)

a.reason: Omitted the G-SIB buffer: 8.25% × 400 = 33.0.

b.reason: Applied the home-country rate to all exposures: 9.5% × 400 = 38.0.

d.reason: Applied the highest national rate: 11.0% × 400 = 44.0.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
questions.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
questions.topic: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
questions.source: Workbook D25.1 • S1, S2, S3 • Map #70
questions.question:
A capital management analyst at a Japanese bank holding company is preparing a briefing for the asset-liability committee on a proposed issue of perpetual contingent convertible bonds. The draft term sheet states:

- Loss absorption: permanent write-down of principal; the bonds never convert into shares
- Trigger: the ratio of Core Tier 1 capital to RWA falls below 7%, or the bank’s primary regulator declares the bank nonviable
- Coupons: non-cumulative

Which of the following statements is correct for the analyst to include in the briefing?

options.text: Because the bonds are written down rather than converted into shares, a trigger event would leave the bank’s equity unchanged and would only reduce its future interest expense.
Because the trigger is defined on Core Tier 1 capital, the bonds would qualify as Additional Tier 1 capital whatever threshold were chosen, including the 4.5% Core Tier 1 minimum.
A trigger event would increase the bank’s equity through the write-down, and with a 7% threshold the bonds can be included in Additional Tier 1 capital rather than Tier 2 capital.
Because the bonds are debt until a trigger event, their holders cannot bear any loss until the bank’s common shareholders have been completely wiped out.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Write-down and equity**

Carey: “With CoCos, equity increases either because the bond converts to equity or because its value is written down.” Writing down the principal removes a liability with no matching asset loss, so equity rises.

**Step 2 – Classification**

“CoCos may be included in Additional Tier 1 Capital if the threshold is 5.125 percent or higher, and Tier 2 capital otherwise”; 7% clears the bar, so the issue counts toward the 6% Tier 1 minimum.

⇒ The write-down design absorbs losses while the bank is still a going concern, which is exactly what the higher AT1 threshold is meant to ensure.

**Interpretation**

C is correct: it combines the S2 point (both mechanisms raise equity) with the S1 point (the 5.125% line).

**LO:** ORR-22 g: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them. ORR-22 d: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: Tier 1 capital and its components; Tier 2 capital and its components; required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital.

- **Reference:** Carey (GARP Risk Institute), Ch.22, 22.3 The Definition of Capital and 22.4 CoCos

ORR-24 • Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms • Vardeez: UNTIERED

**Source:** Workbook D25.1 • S1, S2, S3 • Map #70 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-22 g.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap. It treats the write-down as if only conversion created equity. Both mechanisms increase equity; the write-down simply does it without issuing shares.

b.reason: Scope/condition error. It drops the threshold condition: a Core Tier 1 trigger is necessary but not suﬀicient. A trigger at 4.5%, below 5.125%, would leave the bonds in Tier 2.

d.reason: Absolute claim. Carey says holders “bear losses not so different from those of equity holders when a bank fails”; a principal write-down can wipe out the holders while shareholders retain value, as with the March 2023 Credit Suisse AT1 write-down (outside-source).

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).
questions.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
questions.topic: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.24, Ch.21 and Ch.2
questions.question: A risk analyst at a mid-sized Canadian bank notices that the percentages 12%, 15% and 18% appear both in the Basel II standardized approach (TSA) for operational risk and in the Basel III standardised approach. The head of operational risk asks how the two approaches differ. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: In both approaches the percentages vary by business line, but the Basel III approach applies them to the business indicator instead of gross income.
Like the basic indicator approach, the Basel III approach ignores years in which the relevant income items were negative.
In the TSA the percentages are betas that vary by business line; in the Basel III approach they are marginal coeﬀicients that rise with the size of the business indicator.
In the Basel III approach a bank whose business indicator exceeds EUR 30 billion applies 18% to its whole business indicator.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The TSA**

Gross income of eight business lines, each multiplied by a beta of 12%, 15% or 18% “depending on the perceived riskiness of the underlying business line”.

**Step 2 – The new SA**

The BI is multiplied by marginal coeﬀicients of 12% (up to EUR 1 billion), 15% (1 to 30 billion) and 18% (above 30 billion): “the marginal increase in the BIC resulting from a one unit increase in the BI”.

⇒ Same numbers, different logic: riskiness of the line against size of the bank.

**Interpretation**

GARP Ch.2: the reform “departed from this view, as operational losses incurred in banks’ various lines of business over the past 20 years did not match expectations”, and the rising coeﬀicients recognise that operational risk grows more than proportionally with size.

**LO:** ORR-24 b: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA). • **Reference:** BCBS, Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms (December 2017), GARP ORR Ch.24, 24.2 and Table 24.1; Carey, GARP ORR Ch.21, Capital for Operational Risk; Chapelle, GARP ORR Ch.2, Until January 2023: BIA, TSA, AMA

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.24, Ch.21 and Ch.2 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-24 b.3)

a.reason: The SA has no business-line split; its coeﬀicients depend on the BI bucket.

b.reason: The BIA ignores negative years; the BI uses absolute values year by year (net interest, trading and banking book results), so a loss-making year still adds to it.

d.reason: The coeﬀicients are marginal: 18% applies only to the BI above EUR 30 billion.

questions.topic: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4 and Ch.24
questions.question: An operational risk modeller at a European bank that held AMA approval built its Pillar 1 capital with a loss distribution approach (LDA): Poisson frequency and lognormal severity fitted to internal and external losses, completed in the tail with scenario data, and read at the 99.9th percentile of the one-year aggregate loss. The bank now applies the Basel III standardised approach. Which of the following statements about the LDA is most accurate?

options.text: The LDA remains the Pillar 1 engine: the 99.9th percentile of the aggregate loss distribution now feeds the loss component in place of average losses.
The LDA is now prohibited, since the standardised approach requires banks to stop modelling operational risk losses for any purpose.
The LDA is now used only by bucket 1 banks, which do not include internal loss data in the standardised approach.
The LDA no longer sets Pillar 1 capital, which follows a prescribed formula of the business indicator and average past losses; it can still serve Pillar 2 (ICAAP) capital and stress testing.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where the LDA sat**

The LDA is “the most widespread technique in operational risk modeling”: it was the engine of most AMA models, the Pillar 1 internal model approach.

**Step 2 – What the SA uses instead**

A prescribed formula: BIC from the business indicator, ILM from the loss component, which is 15 times average annual losses over ten years. No percentile is modelled.

**Step 3 – What happens to the models**

GARP Ch.4: with the SA “there are no formal requirements for financial institutions to model their operational risk capital anymore”, but the effort “is now being transferred to modeling Pillar 2 and operational capital requirements under ICAAP, as well as stress testing”.

⇒ D is the accurate statement.

**Interpretation**

This is Vardeez’s “where the LDA sits”: inside the AMA, now outside Pillar 1.

**LO:** ORR-24 b: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA). • **Reference:** Chapelle, GARP ORR Ch.4, 4.4 Operational Risk Modeling and Capital (LDA; Capital Modeling for Operational Risk); BCBS, GARP ORR Ch.24, 24.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.4 and Ch.24 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-24 b.5)

a.reason: The loss component is 15 times average annual losses, not a modelled 99.9th percentile.

b.reason: Absolute claim: banks may still model for Pillar 2, ICAAP and stress testing.

c.reason: Bucket 1 banks have ILM = 1; no bank uses an LDA for Pillar 1.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.
questions.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
questions.topic: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
questions.question:
An operational risk analyst at a German bank with a business indicator of EUR 12 billion is deciding which of last year’s events belong in the standardised approach loss data set. The supervisor has not raised the collection threshold.

I. A EUR 3 million loan loss after a borrower’s collateral was found to be fraudulently overvalued; the loss is already captured in the bank’s credit risk RWA.

II. A EUR 1.2 million trading loss caused by a booking error that left an FX position unhedged.

III. A EUR 15,000 penalty for a late regulatory filing.

IV. A EUR 400,000 loss on loans disbursed to fraudsters using stolen identities, recorded as an operational loss and not reflected in credit risk RWA.

Which of these events should be included?

options.text: II only
II and IV only
I, II and IV only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Credit boundary**

Event I is a credit-related operational loss already accounted for in credit risk RWA: excluded. Event IV is credit-related but not in credit RWA: included.

**Step 2 – Market boundary**

Event II is a market-related operational loss; such losses “are treated as operational risk”: included.

**Step 3 – Threshold**

Event III, EUR 15,000, is below the EUR 20,000 minimum threshold: not in the SA data set (the bank may still record it internally).

⇒ II and IV.

**Interpretation**

The boundary rules stop double counting: a loss already capitalised in credit RWA is not capitalised again. Comprehensiveness (all material activities, subsystems and locations) is checked against that rule set, not against every event the bank ever records.

**LO:** ORR-24 c: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data. • **Reference:** BCBS, Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms (December 2017), GARP ORR Ch.24, 24.5 (d), (f), (g)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.24 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-24 c.5)

a.reason: Drops event IV, which is not in credit RWA and so must be included.

c.reason: Adds event I, which is already in credit RWA.

d.reason: Adds event III, which is below the EUR 20,000 threshold.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.
questions.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
questions.topic: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
questions.question: The head of loss data at a UK bank is drafting the policy for building the standardised approach loss data set. Which of the following rules is consistent with the Basel Committee’s criteria?

options.text: Losses enter the data set on their date of discovery, since that is when the bank becomes aware of the event.
Losses from one event that are posted to the accounts over several years are recorded in full in the year in which the event first occurred.
A legal loss enters the data set no later than the date on which a legal reserve for the probable estimated loss is established in the P&L.
An insurance claim accepted by the insurer is netted against the gross loss as soon as it is lodged, since it is a receivable linked to the event.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The reference date**

“Banks must use the date of accounting for building the loss data set”, and “a date no later than the date of accounting for including losses related to legal events”. For legal events that is the date a legal reserve is established for the probable estimated loss.

⇒ C is consistent with the criteria.

**Step 2 – Grouped losses and recoveries**

Losses posted over several years are allocated to the corresponding years “in line with their accounting treatment”. Recoveries reduce losses only after payment is received.

**Interpretation**

All three dates (occurrence, discovery, accounting) are collected as fields, but only the accounting date decides the year a loss belongs to (Figure 1).

**LO:** ORR-24 c: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data. • **Reference:** BCBS, Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms (December 2017), GARP ORR Ch.24, 24.5 (e) and 24.6

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.24 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-24 c.6)

a.reason: Discovery is a recorded field, not the date that builds the data set.

b.reason: Grouped losses follow their accounting treatment year by year, not the year of occurrence (see the correction box).

d.reason: A lodged claim is a receivable; it cannot be netted until the insurer pays.

questions.loText: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.
questions.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
questions.topic: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
questions.question: A European bank sold its consumer finance subsidiary last year and has just settled a large mis-selling case in a retail business line it still operates. The CFO asks the head of operational risk whether these losses can be removed from the loss component of the standardised approach. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A bank may exclude any loss that it judges no longer relevant to its risk profile, provided the loss is older than five years.
Exclusion needs supervisory approval and should be rare; the bank must show the cause could not recur elsewhere in its operations, and exclusions are disclosed under Pillar 3.
Losses from the divested subsidiary can be excluded only after a minimum retention period in the loss database, typically three years.
Settled legal losses are excluded automatically once paid, since a settled case leaves no residual legal exposure.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The exclusion rule**

Banks “may request supervisory approval to exclude certain operational loss events that are no longer relevant”; exclusion “should be rare and supported by strong justification”. Supervisors consider whether the cause could occur in other areas of the bank’s operations, and expect the bank to show no similar or residual legal exposure.

**Step 2 – Conditions and disclosure**

A materiality threshold (for example, more than 5% of average losses), a minimum retention period in the database (for example, three years) except for divested activities, and Pillar 3 disclosure of the number and amount of exclusions.

⇒ B states the rule.

**Interpretation**

The mis-selling case is in a business line the bank still runs, so a similar loss could recur: exclusion is unlikely. The divested subsidiary’s losses are the stronger candidate, and they skip the retention period.

**LO:** ORR-24 c: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data. • **Reference:** BCBS, Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms (December 2017), GARP ORR Ch.24, 24.7 Exclusion of Losses from the Loss Component

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.24 (Operational Risk and Resilience Workbook, Question ORR-24 c.7)

a.reason: Exclusion is the supervisor’s decision, not the bank’s, and there is no five-year rule.

c.reason: Reversed: losses related to divested activities are not subject to a minimum retention period.

d.reason: Nothing is excluded automatically; the bank must demonstrate there is no similar or residual exposure.
